blocks.html: Earth scientists find it handy to sort everything on our planet into four big parts, called spheres. Each one is a system of its own, and they are all linked.

head: Sphere
What it holds
Examples
rows: Solid Earth: rock, soil and the hot interior
All of Earth's water, liquid and frozen
The layer of gases around Earth
blocks.cap: The four spheres. The prefixes help: geo means earth, hydro water, atmo vapor, bio life.

blocks.html: Earth has four spheres: geosphere (rock), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air) and biosphere (life). Almost every event on Earth moves matter or energy between two or more of them.

The spheres share space and trade materials all the time. Rain falls from the atmosphere into the hydrosphere. Plants (biosphere) pull water out of soil (geosphere) and breathe it into the air (atmosphere). Because matter and energy keep flowing across the boundaries, a change in one sphere usually shows up in the others.

blocks.name: es-water
blocks.cap: Water moving through all four spheres: from the ocean into the air, onto the land, through plants and back to the sea. Press play to watch it move.

blocks.title: Rain on a hillside
blocks.q: Heavy rain washes soil from a hillside into a river. Which spheres are involved?
steps: The rain comes from clouds: atmosphere.
The soil is broken rock and once-living matter: geosphere.
The river is water: hydrosphere.
If the muddy water buries plants or fish eggs, the biosphere is involved too.
blocks.a: At least three: atmosphere, geosphere and hydrosphere

blocks.title: Where does it belong?
blocks.q: Sort a glacier, a volcano's ash cloud and a coral reef.
steps: A glacier is frozen water: hydrosphere.
Ash is tiny bits of rock, so it belongs to the geosphere, even while it floats in the atmosphere.
A coral reef is built by living animals: biosphere (its stony skeleton later becomes part of the geosphere).

blocks.html: Treating each sphere as a separate box. Most real events involve two or more spheres at once. A quick check: for any event, ask "Where did the matter come from, and where did it go?" If the answers name different spheres, they interact.

blocks.html: To find a point on a coordinate plane, you give two numbers. A globe works the same way, with angles instead of distances. The two numbers are latitude and longitude.

items: Latitude tells how far north or south of the equator a place is, from 0° at the equator to 90° at each pole. Lines of latitude run east and west in rings that never meet.
Longitude tells how far east or west of the prime meridian (through Greenwich, England) a place is, from 0° to 180°. Lines of longitude run from pole to pole, and they all meet at the poles.

blocks.html: Write latitude first, then longitude, each with its direction: New Orleans is at about 30° N, 90° W. Latitude says north or south; longitude says east or west.

The equator and the prime meridian act like the x- and y-axes. North and east are like positive numbers, south and west like negative ones, so 30° S, 60° W can also be written (−30, −60). The angles are measured from Earth's center, which is why they stop at 90° (a pole) and 180° (halfway around).

blocks.name: es-earth-sun
blocks.cap: Drag to turn the globe. Rings of latitude never touch; lines of longitude meet at the poles.

blocks.title: Reading a place
blocks.q: Buenos Aires is about 34° south of the equator and 58° west of the prime meridian. Write its location.
steps: Latitude comes first: 34° S.
Longitude second: 58° W.

blocks.title: How far apart?
blocks.q: Two towns lie on the same line of longitude, one at 20° N and one at 15° S. How many degrees of latitude apart are they?
steps: They are on opposite sides of the equator.
From 20° N down to the equator is 20°, then 15° more to 15° S.
$20 + 15 = 35$ degrees. (Each degree of latitude is about 111 km, so that is about 3,900 km.)

blocks.html: Swapping the two, or mixing up which lines meet. Latitude lines are like the rungs of a ladder ("lat" sounds like ladder), parallel and never meeting. Longitude lines are long, running pole to pole, and they all meet at the poles. Check: a latitude can never be more than 90°.

blocks.html: A flat map can show the shape of the land in 3-D with contour lines. Each contour line joins points that are the same height above sea level. Walk along one and you never go up or down.

items: The contour interval is the change in height from one line to the next. It is printed on the map.
Index contours are darker lines with their elevation written on them, often every fifth line.
Lines close together mean a steep slope; lines far apart mean a gentle one.
A set of closed loops is a hill; the smallest loop is the top. Loops with little ticks pointing inward mark a hollow.
Where a stream crosses contour lines, the lines bend into V's that point upstream.

blocks.html: Elevation of a point = the value of its contour line. Count lines between two points and multiply by the interval to find how much higher one is. Close lines mean steep ground.

Picture slicing a hill with flat sheets of glass every 20 m and tracing each slice onto paper from above. Where the hill is steep, you climb 20 m in a short sideways step, so the tracings land close together. On a gentle slope you must walk far to gain 20 m, so they spread out.

blocks.name: es-topo
blocks.cap: Drag the ends of line A–B to see the land's profile. Notice where the contour lines crowd together.

blocks.title: Reading heights
blocks.q: Index contours are labeled 300 m and 400 m, with 4 thinner lines between them. Point P is on the second line above the 300 m index. What is its elevation?
steps: From 300 to 400 there are 5 steps (4 thin lines make 5 gaps).
Interval: $100 \div 5 = 20$ m.
Two lines above 300 m: $300 + 2 \times 20 = 340$ m.

blocks.title: How high is the top?
blocks.q: The highest closed loop on a hill is 460 m and the interval is 20 m. What can you say about the summit?
steps: The summit is above the 460 m line, since that loop surrounds it.
It is below 480 m, or there would be a 480 m loop.
So it is at least 460 m and less than 480 m.

blocks.name: earthsci-contours
blocks.cap: A hill steep on its east side. Change the interval and watch the heights of A and B change, even though the drawing stays the same.

blocks.html: Reading closely spaced lines as flat or low ground. It is the opposite: crowded lines mean the land rises fast, like a cliff. Another slip is taking a contour line for a road or a trail. Check: every contour line has a single height, and two lines never cross.

blocks.html: Every morning the Sun seems to rise in the east, climb across the sky and set in the west. It looks as if the Sun is moving. In fact Earth is spinning, like a merry-go-round under a fixed lamp. Earth turns from west to east once about every 24 hours, and you ride along.
Earth rotates once a day, from west to east. The half facing the Sun has day; the half facing away has night. Because we turn toward the east, the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.

A full turn is 360°, and it takes about 24 hours, so Earth turns $360 \div 24 = 15$ degrees every hour. That steady rate is why time zones are about 15° of longitude wide: places 15° farther east see the Sun reach its highest point one hour earlier.

blocks.name: es-earth-sun
blocks.cap: The lit half of Earth faces the Sun. Press "Turn Earth" or drag the time to watch places move from night into day. The bands show local solar time.

blocks.title: How far in 6 hours?
blocks.q: Through how many degrees does Earth turn in 6 hours?
steps: Earth turns 15° each hour.
$6 \times 15 = 90$ degrees, a quarter turn.

blocks.title: Noon somewhere else
blocks.q: The Sun is at its highest point (solar noon) over a town at 75° W. What is the solar time in a town at 45° W?
steps: The second town is $75 - 45 = 30$ degrees farther east.
Each 15° is one hour: $30 \div 15 = 2$ hours.
Eastern places are ahead, since they turned into the sunlight first: 2:00 p.m.

blocks.html: Saying the Sun travels around Earth each day, or that night comes when clouds or the Moon block the Sun. Night is simply our side of Earth facing away from the Sun. A check: at every moment it is day on one half of Earth and night on the other, which a cloud or the Moon could never do.
Clock time zones follow country and state borders, so they bend around the 15° bands. Solar time is what the Sun itself shows.

blocks.html: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4°, and it keeps pointing the same way in space (toward the North Star) all year. As Earth travels around the Sun, first one hemisphere and then the other leans toward the Sun. This tilt, not our distance from the Sun, makes the days longer or shorter and the Sun higher or lower.

items: Around June 21 the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun: long days and a high noon Sun there (summer), short days in the south (winter).
Around December 21 it is the other way around.
Around March 20 and September 22 (the equinoxes) neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and day and night are close to 12 hours everywhere.

blocks.html: Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets a higher Sun and longer days, so it has summer, while the other hemisphere has winter.

A high Sun is strong sunlight. Shine a flashlight straight down and you get a small, bright spot; tilt it and the same light spreads over a bigger, dimmer patch. When the Sun is high, each square meter of ground gets more energy, and long days give it more hours to collect it. Low Sun and short days add up to winter.

blocks.name: es-earth-sun
blocks.cap: Move the date and watch the axis keep pointing the same way. The Beam tab shows the same sunlight spread over more ground when the Sun is low.

blocks.title: The noon Sun at an equinox
blocks.q: How high is the noon Sun above the horizon at 40° N on March 20?
steps: At an equinox the Sun is overhead at the equator (0°).
Each degree you go away from the equator, the noon Sun is a degree lower: $90 - 40 = 50$.

blocks.title: The noon Sun at a solstice
blocks.q: On June 21 the Sun is overhead at 23.4° N. How high is the noon Sun at 40° N then? And on December 21, when it is overhead at 23.4° S?
steps: June: the place is $40 - 23.4 = 16.6$ degrees from where the Sun is overhead, so the Sun is $90 - 16.6 = 73.4$° high.
December: the place is $40 + 23.4 = 63.4$ degrees away, so the Sun is $90 - 63.4 = 26.6$° high.

blocks.html: Saying summer comes when Earth is closest to the Sun. Earth is closest in early January (about 147 million km) and farthest in early July (about 152 million km), only about 3% different. If distance made the seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time, but Australia has summer in January while the United States has winter.

blocks.html: The Moon makes no light of its own. Sunlight always lights the half of the Moon that faces the Sun, just as it lights the day side of Earth. As the Moon orbits Earth, about once every 29.5 days from new moon to new moon, we see different amounts of that lit half. These changing shapes are the phases.

head: Phase
About how many days after new moon
What we see (Northern Hemisphere)
rows: Nothing: the lit half faces away from us
A thin sliver, lit on the right
A thin sliver on the left
blocks.cap: Waxing means growing; waning means shrinking. From the Southern Hemisphere the Moon looks flipped, lit on the other side.

blocks.html: Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. The phase depends on how much of that lit half faces Earth, which changes as the Moon moves around its orbit.

Hold a ball at arm's length in a room with one lamp, and turn slowly in a circle. When the ball is between you and the lamp you see its dark side (new moon). A quarter turn later you see half lit and half dark (a quarter moon). With the lamp behind you, the whole face you see is lit (full moon). Nothing blocked any light; only your view of the lit half changed.

blocks.name: es-moon
blocks.cap: Drag the Moon around its orbit. The inset shows how it looks from Earth. Turn on Earth's shadow: it points away from the Sun and misses the Moon at every phase except a lined-up full moon.

blocks.title: What comes next?
blocks.q: Tonight the Moon is at first quarter. What will it look like in about a week?
steps: From first quarter it keeps growing (waxing) toward full.
First quarter is about day 7; a week later is about day 14 or 15.

blocks.title: Rising time
blocks.q: A full moon is on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun. About when does it rise?
steps: Opposite the Sun means it comes up as the Sun goes down.
So a full moon rises around sunset and sets around sunrise.

blocks.html: Thinking Earth's shadow makes the phases. Earth's shadow points straight away from the Sun, and it falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, a few times a year. Check: a crescent moon is near the Sun in the sky, where Earth's shadow could never reach it.
Try it in the Night Sky Lab: step through a month and watch the Moon's shape and rising time change.

blocks.html: An eclipse happens when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up, so that one body's shadow falls on another. There are two kinds, and each goes with one phase of the Moon.

items: Solar eclipse: the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, and its shadow falls on Earth. It can happen only at new moon. Totality is seen only along a narrow path.

Lunar eclipse: Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. It can happen only at full moon, and anyone on Earth's night side can see it. The Moon often turns a coppery red.

blocks.html: Solar eclipse: Moon's shadow on Earth, at new moon. Lunar eclipse: Earth's shadow on the Moon, at full moon. They are rare because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to Earth's.

If the Moon's orbit lay flat in the same plane as Earth's, every new moon would block the Sun and every full moon would be eclipsed. But it is tilted about 5°, so most months the Moon passes a little above or below the line from the Sun to Earth, and the shadows miss. Only when a new or full moon happens near one of the two places where the orbits cross (the nodes) do the three line up. That happens in two "eclipse seasons" each year, about six months apart.

blocks.name: es-moon
blocks.cap: The Moon's tilted orbit, seen from the side (the tilt is drawn three times bigger). Change the date: an eclipse happens only when a new or full moon falls near the line where the two orbits cross.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: An eclipse is seen from every place where the Moon is up, and the Moon turns dark red. What kind is it, and what phase is the Moon?
steps: Seen by everyone who can see the Moon: Earth's shadow is on the Moon itself.
That is a lunar eclipse, which needs Earth between the Sun and Moon: a full moon.
blocks.a: A lunar eclipse at full moon

blocks.title: Same size in the sky
blocks.q: The Sun is about 1,392,000 km wide and the Moon about 3,475 km. About how many Moons would fit across the Sun?
steps: The Sun is also about 400 times farther away than the Moon, so the two look nearly the same size. That is why the Moon can just cover the Sun in a total eclipse.

blocks.html: Expecting an eclipse every month. A new moon and a full moon come every month, but the 5° tilt means the shadows usually pass above or below. Check: most full moons are bright and round, with no eclipse at all.
NASA advises that, except during the brief total phase of a total solar eclipse, it is not safe to look directly at the Sun without special eye protection made for solar viewing.

blocks.html: Every object with mass pulls on every other object with mass. This pull is gravity. It is stronger when the masses are bigger and weaker when they are farther apart. Earth's huge mass is why things fall; the Sun's far larger mass holds all the planets.
Gravity pulls masses toward each other. An orbit is falling around a body while moving sideways so fast that you keep missing it.

Imagine a cannon on a very tall mountain. Fire a ball slowly and it curves down and lands. Fire it faster and it lands farther away. Earth is round, so the ground curves away under the ball too. Fire it fast enough (near Earth, about 8 km every second) and the ground curves away exactly as fast as the ball falls. The ball is still falling, but it never lands: it is in orbit. The Moon does the same around Earth, and Earth around the Sun.

blocks.name: ph-orbit
blocks.cap: Newton's cannon. Raise the launch speed: slow balls fall back to Earth; at about 7.9 km/s the ball falls all the way around.

blocks.title: Weight on Mars
blocks.q: Gravity at the surface of Mars is about 0.38 of Earth's. A rover weighs 9,000 N on Earth. What does it weigh on Mars, and what happens to its mass?
steps: Weight is the pull of gravity, so it shrinks with the weaker gravity: $9{,}000 \times 0.38 = 3{,}420$ N.
Mass is the amount of matter. The rover is made of the same stuff, so its mass does not change.

blocks.title: Farther away
blocks.q: A satellite moves from 1 Earth radius from Earth's center (on the ground) to 2 Earth radii. How does Earth's pull on it change?
steps: Gravity weakens with the square of the distance.
Twice as far: $2^2 = 4$, so the pull is $\tfrac{1}{4}$ as strong.

blocks.html: Believing there is no gravity in space, so astronauts float. The space station orbits only about 400 km up, where gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and their station are falling around Earth together, like riders in a falling elevator. Check: without gravity, the station would fly off in a straight line instead of circling Earth.

blocks.html: Along most coasts the sea rises and falls twice a day. These tides come from gravity, mostly the Moon's. The Moon pulls hardest on the side of Earth facing it and weakest on the far side, and that difference stretches Earth's oceans into two bulges.

There are two tidal bulges, one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. As Earth turns, a coast passes through both bulges, so it gets two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours 50 minutes.

The Moon pulls the near-side ocean a bit more than it pulls Earth's center, so that water heaps up toward the Moon. It pulls Earth's center a bit more than the far-side ocean, so Earth is pulled away from that water, leaving a second bulge behind. Why 24 h 50 min and not 24 h? While Earth spins once, the Moon moves along its orbit, so Earth needs about 50 extra minutes to face the Moon again. High tides are about 12 h 25 min apart.

blocks.name: es-moon
blocks.cap: Two bulges of water, drawn much bigger than they really are. Turn on the Sun and move it: lined up with the Moon you get extra-high spring tides; at a right angle, smaller neap tides.

blocks.title: The next high tide
blocks.q: High tide at a harbor is at 3:10 a.m. About when is the next high tide?
steps: High tides come about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
3:10 a.m. plus 12 h is 3:10 p.m.; plus 25 min more is 3:35 p.m.

blocks.title: Spring or neap?
blocks.q: Tonight there is a full moon. Will the tides be bigger or smaller than usual?
steps: At full moon (and new moon) the Sun, Earth and Moon are in a line.
The Sun's smaller tide adds to the Moon's, so highs are higher and lows are lower: spring tides. (The name has nothing to do with the season.)

blocks.html: Picturing one bulge facing the Moon and expecting one high tide a day. There is a second bulge on the far side, so most coasts get two high tides a day. Check: tide tables for most beaches list two highs and two lows each day, each about 50 minutes later than the day before.

blocks.html: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system, and its gravity keeps everything else in orbit. Those other objects fall into a few families.

items: Rocky inner planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. Small, made of rock and metal, with few or no moons.
Giant outer planets: Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants, mostly hydrogen and helium) and Uranus and Neptune (ice giants). Huge, with rings and many moons.
Dwarf planets: round, but too small to clear their orbits of other objects. Pluto, Eris and Ceres are examples.
Asteroids: rocky and metal chunks, most in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
Comets: balls of ice and dust from the far edges of the solar system. Near the Sun they grow tails that point away from the Sun.
Moons: natural objects that orbit a planet or a smaller body, like our Moon or Jupiter's Ganymede.

blocks.html: Four small rocky planets lie close to the Sun; four giant planets lie farther out. Dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and moons fill in the rest.

When the solar system formed, it was too warm near the young Sun for ice to stay frozen, so only rock and metal could clump into the inner planets. Farther out it was cold enough for ice too, so there was far more solid material. The outer planets grew big enough to pull in huge amounts of hydrogen and helium gas, which is why they became giants.

blocks.name: es-scale
blocks.cap: The planets side by side, with their sizes, distances, years and temperatures. Sort by temperature and look where Venus lands.

blocks.title: Which family?
blocks.q: Ceres is round, orbits the Sun in the asteroid belt and shares its orbit with many asteroids. What is it?
steps: It is round and orbits the Sun, like a planet.
But it has not cleared its orbit of other objects.
So it is a dwarf planet (the largest object in the asteroid belt).

blocks.title: The hottest planet
blocks.q: Mercury is about 58 million km from the Sun and Venus about 108 million km. Mercury's average temperature is about 167 °C; Venus's is about 464 °C. Why is Venus hotter?
steps: Being closer to the Sun is not the whole story.
Venus has a very thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide that traps heat (a strong greenhouse effect).
Mercury has almost no air, so its heat escapes quickly, especially at night.
blocks.a: Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat

blocks.html: Guessing that Mercury is the hottest planet because it is closest to the Sun. Venus is hotter everywhere on its surface, day and night, because its thick carbon dioxide air traps heat. Check a planet table from NASA before trusting a guess.

blocks.html: Distances in the solar system are so big that kilometers become clumsy. Astronomers use the astronomical unit (AU), the average distance from Earth to the Sun: about 150 million km. Then you can compare distances with ratios.

head: Planet
Distance from the Sun (AU)
Width compared with Earth
blocks.cap: Rounded from NASA's planetary fact sheets. The Sun is about 109 times as wide as Earth.

blocks.html: 1 AU ≈ 150 million km. In a true scale model, the planets are tiny dots, very far from the Sun and from each other.

A scale model shrinks every length by the same factor, so all the ratios stay true. Shrink the Sun to a ball 1 m wide. Earth, 109 times smaller, becomes about 9 mm across, the size of a pea, and it sits about 107 m away, a whole soccer field. Neptune would be over 3 km away. Pictures in books squeeze the planets close together to fit them on a page.

blocks.name: es-scale
blocks.cap: A true scale model with a 1-meter Sun. Change the Sun's size and watch every distance change with it.

blocks.title: From AU to kilometers
blocks.q: Jupiter is about 5.2 AU from the Sun. About how far is that in kilometers?
steps: 1 AU is about 150 million km.
$5.2 \times 150 = 780$, so about 780 million km.

blocks.title: A model on a field
blocks.q: In a school model, 1 AU is 10 m. How far from the model Sun should Saturn (9.6 AU) go? And Neptune (30.1 AU)?
steps: Each AU is 10 m, so multiply by 10.
Saturn: $9.6 \times 10 = 96$ m. Neptune: $30.1 \times 10 = 301$ m.
blocks.a: Saturn at 96 m, Neptune at 301 m

blocks.html: Trusting book pictures that squeeze the planets together and draw them nearly as big as the Sun. On a true scale, the space between planets is enormous: Earth is about 107 Sun-widths from the Sun. Check: divide distance by size; if a picture fits on a page with visible planets, it can't be to scale.
Light from the Sun takes about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth, 1 AU away. It takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.

blocks.html: Past the planets, distances get so huge that even astronomical units are too small. Astronomers use the light-year: the distance light travels in one year. Light moves about 300,000 km every second, so one light-year is about 9.5 trillion km.

items: The Sun is a star, an ordinary one: medium in size and brightness.
The nearest other star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.
The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy about 100,000 light-years across. We are about 26,000 light-years from its center.
The Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies. The nearest big one, the Andromeda Galaxy, is about 2.5 million light-years away.

blocks.html: A light-year is a distance, about 9.5 trillion km. Stars are light-years apart; galaxies are huge groups of billions of stars, millions of light-years apart.

A light-year sounds like a time, but it is built like "an hour's drive": a distance measured by how far something goes in a set time. It also means we see the past. Light from a star 100 light-years away left it 100 years ago, so we see the star as it was then.

blocks.name: es-scale
blocks.cap: Zoom out from Earth to the planets, the stars and the galaxies. Each step multiplies the size of the view.

blocks.title: In kilometers
blocks.q: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away. About how far is that in kilometers?
steps: 1 light-year is about 9.5 trillion km.
$4.2 \times 9.5 \approx 40$, so about 40 trillion km.

blocks.title: Looking back in time
blocks.q: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away. How old is the light we see from it tonight?
steps: Light covers one light-year in one year.
So it took about 2.5 million years to get here.

blocks.html: Thinking a light-year measures time, or that the stars lie just past the planets. A light-year is a distance. And the nearest star is about 9,000 times farther than Neptune. Check: if the answer to "how far?" is in light-years, it is a distance; the time is in plain years.

blocks.html: Which is heavier, a kilogram of feathers or a kilogram of rock? Neither: they have the same mass. But the feathers take up far more space. Density tells how tightly mass is packed into a space. It is a unit rate: grams for each cubic centimeter.
$$\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}$$ in g/cm³. Water's density is 1 g/cm³. An object floats in a fluid if it is less dense than the fluid, and sinks if it is denser.

A floating object pushes water out of the way. The water pushes back up with a force equal to the weight of the water moved aside. If the object is less dense than water, it only has to sink partway before it has moved its own weight of water, so it floats. A denser object can't move enough water even when it is all the way under, so it sinks. The same rule sorted Earth: dense iron sank to the middle, and light rock rose to the top.

blocks.name: es-density
blocks.cap: Drop blocks of different materials into the tank and change the fluid. A block floats when it is less dense than the fluid, whatever its size. The Column tab stacks fluids by density.

blocks.title: Density of a rock
blocks.q: A rectangular block of granite is 3 cm by 4 cm by 5 cm and has a mass of 162 g. What is its density?
steps: Volume of a rectangular prism: $3 \times 4 \times 5 = 60$ cm³.
Density: $162 \div 60 = 2.7$ g/cm³.
That is denser than water (1 g/cm³), so granite sinks.

blocks.title: How much is underwater?
blocks.q: Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³. What fraction of a floating ice cube sits below the water line in fresh water?
steps: A floating object sinks until it has moved its own weight of water.
Fraction under = density of object ÷ density of fluid = $0.92 \div 1.00 = 0.92$.
So about 92% is under water and only about 8% sticks out.

blocks.html: Saying heavy things sink and light things float. That mixes up mass with density. A huge log is heavy, yet it floats because wood is less dense than water; a tiny pebble sinks because rock is denser. Check: compare densities in g/cm³, not masses.

blocks.html: Earth is layered like a peach: a thin skin, a thick middle and a dense pit. The layers formed when young Earth was hot enough for its materials to sort by density: iron sank and lighter rock floated up.

head: Layer
Depth (km)
Made of
Solid or liquid
Density (g/cm³)
rows: Light rock: granite in continents, basalt under oceans
Hot rock rich in iron and magnesium
blocks.cap: Earth's layers by what they are made of. Rounded values.

blocks.html: Earth has four main layers: a thin rocky crust, a thick solid mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Density increases toward the center.

No one has drilled past the crust; the deepest hole is about 12 km. We know the layers from earthquake waves. Waves speed up, slow down and bend as they pass through different materials, and one kind of wave (S waves) cannot travel through liquid. S waves never cross the outer core, so it must be liquid. Earth's average density, about 5.5 g/cm³, is twice that of surface rock, so the inside must be much denser.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: Drag the probe from the surface to the center and read the depth, temperature, pressure and whether the rock is solid or liquid.

blocks.title: Which layer?
blocks.q: A probe reads a depth of 4,000 km. Which layer is it in?
steps: The mantle ends at about 2,900 km.
The outer core runs from 2,900 to 5,150 km, and 4,000 km is between them.

blocks.title: How thick?
blocks.q: Using the table, how thick is the outer core?
steps: It starts at 2,900 km and ends at 5,150 km.

blocks.html: Picturing the mantle as a sea of liquid magma. The mantle is almost entirely solid rock; it is so hot that it can creep very slowly, a few centimeters a year, like very stiff putty. Only the outer core is liquid. Check: S waves pass through the mantle, which they could not do if it were liquid.

sources.name: OpenStax, Astronomy 2e, 8.1 The Global Perspective

Dziewonski and Anderson (1981), Preliminary Reference Earth Model (densities, rounded)

blocks.html: The crust, mantle and core describe what Earth is made of. Geologists also sort the outer layers by how they behave: are they stiff and brittle, or soft and able to flow?

items: Lithosphere ("stone sphere"): the crust plus the cold, stiff top of the mantle, about 100 km thick on average (thinner under oceans, thicker under old continents). It is broken into the tectonic plates.
Asthenosphere ("weak sphere"): hot, soft mantle rock below the lithosphere, down to a few hundred kilometers. It is solid, but it can slowly flow.

blocks.html: Tectonic plates are pieces of lithosphere: crust plus the uppermost mantle. They slide over the hot, weak but solid asthenosphere.

Whether rock bends, breaks or flows depends on how hot it is. Near the surface the rock is cool and brittle, so it cracks. Deeper down it is close to its melting point. It stays solid, but over thousands of years it can creep, like a candle that is warm but not melted. The boundary between stiff and soft rock lies inside the mantle, so the lithosphere includes the crust and the top of the mantle.

blocks.name: es-interior
blocks.cap: The same Earth sorted by behavior. The crust is drawn ten times thicker so you can see it. Notice that the lithosphere reaches below the crust into the mantle.

blocks.title: Under the crust
blocks.q: Under a continent, the crust is 35 km thick and the lithosphere is 120 km thick. How much of the lithosphere is mantle rock?
steps: The lithosphere is the crust plus the top of the mantle.
$120 - 35 = 85$ km of it is mantle.

blocks.title: Two ways to name a layer
blocks.q: Rock 200 km below the surface is in which compositional layer, and which behavior layer?
steps: The crust is at most about 70 km thick, so 200 km down is the mantle.
The lithosphere is about 100 km thick, so 200 km down is below it, in the soft asthenosphere.

blocks.html: Thinking the plates are only crust, or that they float on liquid. Plates are lithosphere: crust plus the top of the mantle, about 100 km thick. They ride on asthenosphere that is hot and weak but still solid. Check: earthquake S waves travel through the asthenosphere, so it can't be a liquid layer.

blocks.html: Heat a pot of soup from below and the soup starts to turn over on its own. Warm soup comes up in the middle and cooler soup slides down the sides. This loop is convection, and it is driven by density.
Warm fluid expands and becomes less dense, so cooler, denser fluid sinks and pushes it up. Heating below and cooling above keep the loop, a convection current, going.

Heat makes particles move faster and spread apart, so the same mass takes up more space: lower density. Gravity pulls the denser, cooler fluid down harder, and it sinks under the warm fluid, shoving it upward. At the top the warm fluid loses heat, becomes denser and sinks in turn. Without gravity there would be no convection: on the space station, a candle flame doesn't rise.

blocks.name: es-density
blocks.cap: Warm fluid (red) rises over the heat and cool fluid (blue) sinks at the sides. Try the mantle scenario too.

items: Air: sunlight warms the ground, warm air rises and cooler air moves in. This makes wind and many clouds.
Ocean: cold, salty water near the poles sinks and creeps along the sea floor.
Mantle: hot rock deep down slowly rises and cooler rock sinks, a few centimeters a year. This slow churning helps move the tectonic plates.

blocks.title: Where does it rise?
blocks.q: A pan of water is heated by a burner under its center. Where does water rise and where does it sink?
steps: Water over the burner warms, expands and becomes less dense.
Cooler, denser water near the sides sinks and flows in along the bottom, pushing the warm water up.
blocks.a: It rises over the burner and sinks at the sides

blocks.title: A slow loop
blocks.q: Mantle rock in a convection loop creeps about 5 cm a year. About how long does it take to move 1,000 km?

blocks.html: Saying "heat rises," as if heat were a substance that floats up. Heat can spread in any direction. In convection, warm fluid rises only because the denser, cooler fluid around it sinks and pushes it up. Check: put the heater at the top of a pot instead, and the water barely circulates.

blocks.html: Rocks are the solid stuff of the geosphere, and minerals are what rocks are made of. Granite, for example, is a mix of the minerals quartz, feldspar and mica. To count as a mineral, a substance must pass five tests.

items: Naturally occurring: formed by nature, not made in a factory or lab.
Inorganic: not made by living things.
Solid at Earth's surface temperatures.
Definite chemical makeup: a fixed recipe of elements, such as SiO₂ for quartz or NaCl for halite (rock salt).
Orderly crystal structure: its atoms are lined up in a repeating pattern.

blocks.html: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical makeup and an orderly crystal structure. A rock is usually a mixture of minerals.

The crystal structure is why minerals have regular shapes. In halite, sodium and chloride ions stack in a cube pattern, so salt grains are tiny cubes and break into smaller cubes. The atoms in volcanic glass are jumbled because the lava froze too fast for them to line up, so glass breaks along smooth curves and is not a mineral.

blocks.name: es-minerals
blocks.cap: A mineral sample on the test bench. The Silicates tab shows how silicon and oxygen atoms link into the orderly patterns of the most common minerals.

blocks.title: Ice and glass
blocks.q: Is the ice in a glacier a mineral? Is window glass?
steps: Glacier ice: natural, not made by living things, solid, always H₂O, and its molecules form a six-sided crystal pattern. It passes all five tests.
Window glass is made in factories, and its atoms are not in an orderly pattern. It fails two tests.
blocks.a: Glacier ice is a mineral; window glass is not

blocks.title: Coal
blocks.q: Coal is a natural solid dug from the ground. Why is it not a mineral?
steps: Coal formed from the remains of ancient plants, so it is organic.
Its makeup varies from place to place, and it has no single crystal pattern.
blocks.a: It comes from living things and has no definite makeup or crystal structure

blocks.html: Calling any rock, gem or crystal a mineral. Granite is a rock (a mixture of minerals), coal and amber come from living things, and glass has no crystal structure. Meanwhile ice, which few people think of, counts. Check each of the five tests one at a time.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, FAQ: What is the difference between a rock and a mineral?

Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-1

blocks.html: Geologists identify a mineral with a few simple tests. Each test measures something set by the mineral's chemistry and crystal structure.

items: Hardness: what it can scratch. The Mohs scale ranks ten minerals from talc (1) to diamond (10). A fingernail is about 2.5, a copper coin 3.5, a steel nail or glass 5.5.
Streak: the color of its powder, made by rubbing it on unglazed white tile.
Luster: how its surface reflects light: metallic or nonmetallic (glassy, pearly, earthy).
Cleavage or fracture: whether it splits along flat planes (cleavage) or breaks along rough or curved surfaces (fracture).
Density: galena (7.5 g/cm³) feels far heavier than quartz (2.65 g/cm³) of the same size.
Special tests: magnetite attracts a magnet; calcite fizzes in weak acid.

blocks.html: Identify minerals with several tests together: hardness, streak, luster, cleavage and density. Color alone can fool you.

Color often comes from tiny traces of other elements. Pure quartz is clear, but a little iron makes it purple (amethyst). Streak is more reliable, because powdering the mineral spreads out those traces: hematite can be steel gray or red-brown in a chunk, yet its streak is always red-brown. Hardness depends on how strongly the atoms are bonded, which is the same in every sample.

blocks.name: es-minerals
blocks.cap: A mystery mineral. Run the tests one at a time and watch the identification table narrow down.

blocks.title: Narrowing hardness
blocks.q: A mineral scratches glass (5.5) but cannot scratch quartz (7). Quartz scratches it. What can you say about its hardness?
steps: It scratches glass, so it is harder than 5.5.
Quartz scratches it, so it is softer than 7.
Its hardness is between 5.5 and 7, so it might be orthoclase feldspar (6).

blocks.title: Same color, different minerals
blocks.q: Two shiny gold-colored samples: A leaves a greenish-black streak and B leaves a golden-yellow streak and bends like soft metal. Which is gold?
steps: Gold's streak is golden yellow, and it is soft (2.5 to 3).
A greenish-black streak and a brassy color mark pyrite, "fool's gold".
blocks.a: B is gold; A is pyrite

blocks.html: Identifying minerals by color, or reading Mohs 10 as ten times harder than 1. One mineral can come in many colors, so use streak and other tests. And the Mohs scale is only a ranking, like places in a race: diamond (10) is far more than ten times as hard as talc, and the steps are not equal. Check: say "harder than" or "softer than," not "twice as hard."

U.S. Geological Survey, FAQ: What is the difference between a rock and a mineral?

blocks.html: Deep in the crust and upper mantle, rock can melt into magma. When magma or lava cools, mineral crystals grow and lock together into igneous rock ("igneous" means "from fire").

head: Where it cooled
How fast
Texture
Examples
rows: Coarse: crystals big enough to see
Fine: crystals too small to see
At the surface, almost at once
At the surface, full of gas
blocks.cap: Texture tells how fast the rock cooled; color tells what it is made of (light rocks are rich in silica).

blocks.html: Slow cooling grows large crystals (intrusive rock like granite); fast cooling makes small crystals (extrusive rock like basalt); very fast cooling makes glass.

Crystals grow as atoms in the melt find their places and join a growing crystal. That takes time. Deep underground, surrounding rock keeps magma warm for thousands of years, so a few crystals grow large. Lava at the surface loses heat quickly, so many tiny crystals start at once and none gets big. If lava freezes in seconds, the atoms stay jumbled: glass.

blocks.name: es-igneous
blocks.cap: Pick where the magma cools and watch crystals grow. Deep plutons grow big crystals; lava in water freezes to glass.

blocks.title: Big crystals
blocks.q: A rock has large, interlocking pink, white and gray crystals. Where did it form?
steps: Large crystals need slow cooling.
Slow cooling happens deep underground, so this is an intrusive rock (it sounds like granite).

blocks.title: Two sizes
blocks.q: A rock has a few large crystals scattered in a fine-grained background. What happened?
steps: The big crystals grew slowly while the magma was still deep.
Then the magma rose and erupted, and the rest cooled fast into tiny crystals.
This two-stage texture is called porphyritic.
blocks.a: Slow cooling underground, then fast cooling at the surface

blocks.html: Expecting fast cooling to make big crystals. Crystals need time to grow, so it is the reverse: slow cooling makes big crystals, and lava that cools in seconds can become glass with no crystals at all. Check: the coarse rocks (granite, gabbro) are the ones found where deep rock has been exposed.

blocks.cap: Igneous rocks sorted by texture (rows) and composition (columns).

blocks.html: Rock at the surface breaks into pieces, called sediment: gravel, sand, silt and clay. Water, wind and ice carry the pieces away and drop them, often in flat layers. Over time the layers become sedimentary rock, made from bits of older rock or from minerals that come out of water.

items: Weathering breaks rock into sediment.
Erosion carries it away.
Deposition drops it in layers, often in lakes and seas.
Compaction: layers piled on top squeeze out water and press the grains together.
Cementation: minerals left by water (often calcite or silica) glue the grains together.

head: Grain size
Sediment
Rock
rows: Conglomerate (breccia if the pieces are sharp-edged)
blocks.cap: Rocks made of pieces (clastic rocks) are named by grain size. Others form from minerals left by water (rock salt, some limestone) or from living things (coal, shell limestone).

blocks.html: Sediment becomes rock when it is buried, squeezed (compaction) and glued by natural cement (cementation). Rocks made of grains are named by their grain size.

Under 1 km of sediment, the weight on each grain is huge. It pushes grains closer and squeezes out water. Water still flowing through the pores carries dissolved minerals, which crystallize between the grains like glue. Drying alone does neither: a pile of dry sand on a beach is still loose sand.

blocks.name: es-rock-key
blocks.cap: Sedimentary rocks sorted by what they are made of and grain size.

blocks.title: Name it by size
blocks.q: A rock is made of rounded grains about 0.5 mm across, cemented together. What is it?
steps: 0.5 mm is between 1/16 mm (about 0.06 mm) and 2 mm.
That is sand-sized, so the rock is sandstone.

blocks.title: Rounded or sharp?
blocks.q: Two rocks are both made of pebbles 1 to 3 cm across. In one the pebbles are rounded; in the other they are sharp-edged. Name both.
steps: Pebbles are gravel-sized (over 2 mm).
Rounded gravel: conglomerate. Its pebbles were tumbled a long way by water.
Angular gravel: breccia. Its pieces did not travel far.

blocks.name: es-sediment
blocks.cap: Grains carried farther by a river get smaller and rounder. Slide the distance.

blocks.html: Thinking sediment turns into rock just by drying out. It takes burial under more layers (compaction) and natural cement deposited by water (cementation). Check: mud left in the sun cracks and crumbles; it does not become shale.

blocks.html: Bury a rock deep, heat it, squeeze it, and it changes, even though it never melts. That is a metamorphic rock ("changed form"). The heat and pressure come from deep burial, from nearby magma, or from plates pushing together. The starting rock can be igneous, sedimentary or even another metamorphic rock.

head: Starting rock
Metamorphic rock
Texture
rows: Slate, then phyllite, schist and gneiss as heat and pressure rise
Foliated: minerals lined up in layers or bands
Not foliated: very hard, quartz grains fused
blocks.cap: Common metamorphic rocks and the rocks they come from.

blocks.html: Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change a rock's minerals and texture while it stays solid. Squeezing often lines minerals up into layers (foliation).

Atoms in a solid can slowly move and rearrange. At high temperature and pressure, some minerals are no longer stable, and their atoms regroup into new minerals that are, such as mica or garnet. When rock is squeezed harder in one direction, flat minerals like mica grow at right angles to the push, so they line up in sheets. That is why slate splits into flat slabs.

blocks.name: es-rock-key
blocks.cap: Metamorphic rocks sorted by texture and grade (how much heat and pressure).

blocks.title: From limestone
blocks.q: Limestone near a hot granite intrusion is baked. What rock forms?
steps: Limestone is made of calcite.
Heat recrystallizes the calcite into larger, interlocking crystals: marble.

blocks.title: Rising grade
blocks.q: Order these by how much heat and pressure they formed under, lowest first: schist, slate, gneiss.
steps: Slate forms at low grade from shale: tiny mica crystals.
Schist forms at higher grade: mica crystals big enough to sparkle.
Gneiss forms at the highest grade: minerals sorted into bands.

blocks.html: Thinking metamorphic rock forms by melting. If a rock melts, it becomes magma, and when that cools it is igneous rock. Metamorphism happens while the rock stays solid. Check: metamorphic rocks still show bent layers and stretched pebbles, which melting would erase.

sources.name: MIT OpenCourseWare, 12.001 Introduction to Geology (metamorphic rocks)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-1

blocks.html: The three rock families, igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic, are linked. Rock is never used up; it is recycled from one kind into another. The pathways together are the rock cycle.

items: Melting turns any rock into magma; cooling turns magma into igneous rock.
Weathering and erosion break any rock that reaches the surface into sediment; deposition, compaction and cementation turn sediment into sedimentary rock.
Heat and pressure turn any rock into metamorphic rock, without melting it.

blocks.html: Any rock can become any other kind. Earth's inner heat drives melting, metamorphism and uplift; sunlight (through wind, rain and ice) and gravity drive weathering and erosion.

Two engines run the cycle. Heat from inside Earth melts rock, bakes it and pushes it up into mountains. At the surface, the Sun's energy drives the water cycle and wind, which break rock down and carry the pieces downhill under gravity. Because both engines keep running, rock keeps moving around the cycle, by whatever path the conditions allow.

blocks.name: es-rock-cycle
blocks.cap: Move a rock around the cycle by choosing a process. Try to get from igneous to metamorphic without passing through sediment.

blocks.title: A shortcut
blocks.q: Gneiss (metamorphic) is pushed up into a mountain and worn down by rain and ice. What does it become next?
steps: Weathering and erosion break any exposed rock into sediment.
So the gneiss becomes sediment, skipping magma and igneous rock completely.

blocks.title: A long trip
blocks.q: Sand from weathered granite is buried and cemented, then squeezed and heated deep in a mountain belt. Name each rock along the way.
steps: Granite is igneous. Weathering makes sand (sediment).
Burial and cementation make sandstone (sedimentary).
Heat and pressure turn sandstone into quartzite (metamorphic).

blocks.html: Learning the cycle as one fixed loop, igneous to sedimentary to metamorphic and back. Rocks can skip steps or go backward: metamorphic rock can weather straight into sediment, and igneous rock can be metamorphosed without ever becoming sediment. Check: for any rock, ask what would happen if it were melted, buried or uplifted, and follow that arrow.

MIT OpenCourseWare, 12.001 Introduction to Geology
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-1

blocks.html: Every rock that reaches the surface starts to fall apart. This breaking down of rock where it sits is weathering, the first step of the rock cycle's trip to sediment. It comes in two kinds.

head: Mechanical weathering: smaller pieces, same minerals
Chemical weathering: new substances
rows: Frost wedging: water in a crack freezes, expands about 9% and pries the rock apart.
Dissolving: rainwater is a weak acid that slowly dissolves limestone, carving caves.
Oxidation: iron in minerals combines with oxygen and rusts, turning rock red-brown.
Abrasion: rocks are worn by sand blown in wind or tumbled in rivers.
Clay formation: water slowly changes feldspar into soft clay.
Unloading: rock buried deep expands when the rock above wears away, and peels in sheets.
Acids from living things: lichens and plant roots give off acids that eat at rock.
blocks.cap: The two kinds of weathering. They usually work together.

blocks.html: Weathering breaks rock down where it is. Mechanical weathering breaks it into smaller pieces of the same stuff; chemical weathering changes its minerals into new substances.

Rocks formed deep underground, under high heat and pressure and without air. At the surface the conditions are very different: cold and warm days, water, oxygen and living things. Minerals that were stable deep down are not stable up here, so they slowly change into ones that are, like clay and rust. And water seeping into cracks, freezing and thawing, pries the rock apart.

blocks.name: es-weathering
blocks.cap: Choose a process and a climate, and watch the rock weather. Notice which processes make new substances and which only make smaller pieces.

blocks.title: Ice in a crack
blocks.q: Water fills a crack in a granite boulder and freezes every winter night. After years the boulder splits in two. What kind of weathering is this?
steps: The pieces are still granite: no new substances formed.
Freezing water widened the crack. This is frost wedging, a kind of mechanical weathering.

blocks.title: A rusty cliff
blocks.q: Gray rock rich in iron slowly turns red-brown and crumbly. What kind of weathering is this?
steps: The color change means a new substance formed: iron oxide (rust).
Iron combining with oxygen is oxidation, a kind of chemical weathering.

blocks.html: Mixing up weathering with erosion. Weathering is the breaking down of rock in place; erosion is the carrying away of the pieces by water, wind, ice or gravity. Check: ask "Did anything move?" If the pieces were carried off, that part is erosion.

sources.name: MIT OpenCourseWare, 12.001 Introduction to Geology (weathering)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-2

blocks.html: Some rocks crumble in decades; others last for millions of years. Weathering speeds up with three things: more surface area, a warm, wet climate, and minerals that break down easily.
Weathering attacks surfaces, so breaking a rock into smaller pieces exposes more surface and speeds it up. Warm, wet climates weather rock fastest, and limestone weathers faster than granite.

Water, oxygen and acids can only reach a rock's outside. Cut a cube in half along every edge and you get 8 smaller cubes. The outside of the big cube is still there, but each cut adds new faces. Using surface area: a 2 cm cube has $6 \times 2^2 = 24$ cm² of surface. Eight 1 cm cubes have $8 \times 6 \times 1^2 = 48$ cm², twice as much, from the same amount of rock.

blocks.name: es-weathering
blocks.cap: Cut the cube more times and watch the total surface area grow while the volume stays the same.

blocks.title: More cuts
blocks.q: A 3 cm cube is cut into 1 cm cubes. How many cubes are there, and how much surface area do they have in all?
steps: Each edge is cut into 3 pieces, so there are $3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27$ cubes.
Each small cube has $6 \times 1^2 = 6$ cm². All together: $27 \times 6 = 162$ cm².
The big cube had $6 \times 3^2 = 54$ cm², so the surface grew 3 times.

blocks.title: Which weathers fastest?
blocks.q: Which weathers fastest: granite in a cold, dry desert; limestone in a warm, rainy forest; or granite in a warm, rainy forest?
steps: Warm, wet places speed up chemical weathering.
Limestone dissolves in rainwater; granite's minerals resist much better.
So limestone in a warm, rainy forest weathers fastest.
blocks.a: Limestone in a warm, rainy forest

blocks.html: Not expecting that breaking a rock exposes more surface. Breaking does not change how much rock there is, but every break opens new faces to water and air. Check with numbers: one 2 cm cube has 24 cm² of surface, but cut into eight 1 cm cubes it has 48 cm².
Cold climates have one fast process of their own: frost wedging, wherever water freezes and thaws over and over.

sources.name: MIT OpenCourseWare, 12.001 Introduction to Geology (weathering)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-2

blocks.html: Soil is not just dirt. It is a mixture of weathered rock, water, air and humus, the dark matter left by dead plants and animals. A healthy soil is roughly half solid (mostly rock grains, with a little humus) and half pore space filled with water and air.

items: O horizon: fallen leaves and other organic matter on top.
A horizon (topsoil): dark, rich in humus, full of roots and living things.
B horizon (subsoil): lighter, with clay and minerals washed down from above.
C horizon: broken, weathered pieces of the rock below.
R: solid bedrock.

blocks.html: Soil forms slowly, from the top down, as bedrock weathers and living things add organic matter. The layers that form are called horizons: O, A, B, C, then bedrock.

Weathering is fastest near the surface, where water, air and roots reach, so rock breaks down there first and the soil deepens over time. Plants grow, die and decay, adding humus at the top, which makes topsoil dark. Rainwater soaking down carries clay and dissolved minerals from the top layer into the next, building the subsoil. That is why horizons stack in the same order nearly everywhere.

blocks.name: es-weathering
blocks.cap: Slide the time to watch soil horizons form on bare rock. Each horizon thickens as weathering and living things do their work.

blocks.title: Air in the soil
blocks.q: A 2,000 cm³ scoop of garden soil is about 25% air. How much air is in it?
steps: 25% is one quarter.
$2{,}000 \times 0.25 = 500$ cm³ of air.

blocks.title: Reading a soil pit
blocks.q: In a soil pit you see, from the top: dark crumbly soil full of roots, then reddish clay-rich soil, then broken chunks of rock. Name them.
steps: Dark, with humus and roots: A horizon (topsoil).
Clay and minerals washed down: B horizon (subsoil).
Broken rock: C horizon. Bedrock would be below.

blocks.html: Thinking soil is just dirt that was always there. Soil forms from rock, water, air and living things over long times; in many places a few centimeters of topsoil took centuries or more to build. That is why losing topsoil to erosion is hard to undo. Check: the bottom of a soil pit almost always shows broken rock, the soil's parent material.

Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-2

blocks.html: After weathering breaks rock into sediment, something has to move it. Erosion is the carrying away of sediment by moving water, wind, ice or gravity. Wherever the carrier slows down, it drops the sediment: deposition.
Moving water, wind and ice pick up sediment and carry it; when they slow down, they drop it, largest grains first. Every grain eroded somewhere is deposited somewhere else.

The faster water or wind moves, the bigger the grains it can push or hold up. A flooded mountain stream rolls boulders; a slow river carries only fine mud. When a river enters a lake, it slows down, so it drops gravel first, near the shore, then sand, then silt, and the finest clay settles far out in calm water. This sorting by size is a fingerprint of water and wind.

blocks.name: es-sediment
blocks.cap: A river flows into a lake and slows down. Watch the largest grains settle first. Change the river's speed.

items: Water (the biggest mover): river deltas, sandbars, beaches, floodplains.
Wind: sand dunes and layers of windblown dust.
Ice: glaciers scrape up rock of every size and drop it in heaps called moraines.
Gravity: landslides, rockfalls and slow soil creep down slopes.

blocks.title: A delta
blocks.q: A muddy river flows into the sea. What forms at its mouth, and why?
steps: The river slows down as it spreads into the still sea.
Slower water can't carry as much sediment, so it drops it, building a delta.
blocks.a: A delta, because the water slows and drops sediment

blocks.title: Which settles first?
blocks.q: A fast stream carrying gravel, sand and clay flows into a pond. In what order do they settle?
steps: Big, heavy grains need fast water to stay moving.
So the gravel drops first, then the sand, and the clay last, far from the inlet.

blocks.html: Thinking erosion only destroys land. Every grain carried away is set down somewhere, building deltas, beaches, dunes and floodplains. Check: the Mississippi Delta is made of sediment eroded from much of the central United States.

blocks.html: Each agent of erosion and deposition leaves its own marks on the land. Learn them, and a landscape (or a topographic map) tells you what shaped it.

head: Agent
Erosion makes
Deposition makes
rows: Floodplains, deltas, sandbars; oxbow lakes from cut-off bends
U-shaped valleys, sharp peaks (horns), bowl-shaped hollows (cirques), scratched bedrock
Moraines and scattered boulders (erratics), all unsorted
Polished, pitted rocks; hollows where sand was blown away
Sand dunes; layers of windblown dust
blocks.cap: Landforms and the agents that make them.

blocks.html: Rivers cut V-shaped valleys and drop sorted sediment; glaciers carve U-shaped valleys and drop unsorted piles; wind builds dunes.

A river cuts only along its narrow bed, down into the rock, while the valley sides slump in: a V. A glacier is a huge tongue of ice that fills the whole valley and grinds its floor and sides at once, rounding it into a U. And because ice is solid, it carries boulders, sand and clay together and drops them together when it melts. Water and wind sort grains by size; ice does not.

blocks.name: es-landscape
blocks.cap: A river grows meanders until one is cut off as an oxbow lake. The Glacier and Wind tabs show their own landforms.

blocks.title: Reading a valley
blocks.q: A mountain valley has a broad, rounded floor with steep sides, and its floor is scattered with boulders of rock found only far upstream. What shaped it?
steps: A broad U shape points to a glacier.
Boulders of distant rock are glacial erratics, carried by ice.

blocks.title: Sorted or not?
blocks.q: Deposit 1 has neat layers of sand. Deposit 2 is a jumble of clay, sand, pebbles and boulders. Which was left by a melting glacier?
steps: Water and wind sort grains by size into layers.
Ice drops everything together, so the unsorted jumble is glacial till.

blocks.html: Expecting glacier deposits to be sorted by size like river deposits. Ice drops boulders, sand and clay together in one jumble, called till. Check: if a deposit has big boulders sitting in fine clay, think ice; neat layers of one grain size point to water or wind.

sources.name: MIT OpenCourseWare, 12.001 Introduction to Geology (rivers and glaciers)
U.S. Geological Survey, Water Science School: Ice, Snow, and Glaciers and the Water Cycle
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-2

blocks.html: Most changes to Earth's surface are too slow to see: a river deepens its canyon by a fraction of a millimeter a year. But a fraction of a millimeter, repeated for millions of years, adds up to a canyon. It is a rate problem: total change = rate × time. A few erosion events, like landslides, happen in minutes.

Total change = rate × time. Tiny yearly changes, kept up for millions of years, build canyons and wear down mountains; a few events, like landslides, floods and eruptions, change the land in minutes or days.

Deep time is hard to picture because our lives are so short. If a river cuts down 0.3 mm a year, you would never notice it in a lifetime: about 2.5 cm in 80 years. But 6 million years is 75,000 lifetimes. Multiply: $0.3 \times 6{,}000{,}000 = 1{,}800{,}000$ mm, which is 1,800 m, about as deep as the Grand Canyon.

blocks.name: es-deep-time
blocks.cap: Choose a rate and a length of time and see how far it adds up.

blocks.title: Unit by unit
blocks.q: A mountain range wears down by about 0.05 mm a year. How much lower is it after 10 million years, in meters?

blocks.title: How long?
blocks.q: A river cuts a 600 m deep canyon at about 0.2 mm a year. About how long did that take?
steps: Change to millimeters: $600 \times 1{,}000 = 600{,}000$ mm.

blocks.html: Thinking big landforms like canyons must come from one sudden event, because tiny yearly changes are hard to picture adding up. Check by multiplying the rate by the time: small rates over millions of years give hundreds or thousands of meters. Fast events do happen too, but they reshape a slope or a valley floor, not a whole canyon.

Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-2

blocks.html: A fossil is the remains or a trace of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock. Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock, because only gently settling sediment can bury a shell or a bone without destroying it.

items: Body fossils: hard parts like shells, bones and teeth, often with minerals filling their pores.
Molds and casts: a shell dissolves and leaves a hollow (a mold); minerals fill the hollow and make a copy (a cast).
Petrified wood: minerals replace wood bit by bit, copying even its cells.
Preserved remains: insects in amber, mammoths in frozen ground.
Trace fossils: footprints, burrows and other signs an animal left behind.

blocks.html: Fossils form when remains or traces of life are buried quickly in sediment before they rot or are eaten. They show what lived long ago, what the environment was like, and which rock layers are the same age.

A dead animal on the ground is soon eaten, rotted or scattered. Quick burial in mud or sand cuts it off from scavengers and from oxygen, which decay needs. Hard parts last longest, so shells, bones and teeth are by far the most common fossils, and soft creatures like jellyfish are rare. Because the conditions are so special, only a tiny share of all living things ever became fossils.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Three rock columns from different places. Tap a layer and then the matching layer next door to draw a tie line. Fossils and the volcanic ash bed are the best guides.

blocks.title: What does it tell us?
blocks.q: Fossil clams and corals are found in limestone near the top of a mountain. What does that tell you?
steps: Clams and corals live in the sea.
So the rock formed on a sea floor and was later lifted up into a mountain.
blocks.a: The area was once under the sea

blocks.title: A good index fossil
blocks.q: Which makes a better index fossil for dating layers: a snail species that lived for 200 million years in one small lake, or a sea creature found all over the world that lived for only 2 million years?
steps: An index fossil must be easy to find in many places: widespread and common.
It must also have lived for only a short time, so finding it pins down a narrow age.
The widespread, short-lived sea creature wins.

blocks.html: Thinking most living things become fossils. Only a tiny share do, mostly those with hard parts that were buried quickly in sediment. Check: think how many animals die in a forest each year, and how few bones you ever find lying around.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, Fossils, Rocks, and Time (online edition)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS1-4

blocks.html: Sediment settles in flat layers, one on top of another, like pages added to the top of a stack. So in sedimentary rock the layers record time from the bottom up. This idea, written down by Nicolaus Steno in 1669, is the law of superposition.

In layers that have not been overturned, the oldest layer is at the bottom and the youngest is at the top. Sediment is also laid down in flat (horizontal) layers, so tilted or folded layers were moved later.

A layer can only settle on something that is already there. The bottom layer had to exist before anything could pile on top of it, so it is older. This gives relative age: which is older or younger, not how many years old. Finding the age in years takes a radioactive clock.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Step through the history one event at a time. Each new layer settles on top of the ones before.

blocks.title: Reading a cliff
blocks.q: A cliff shows, from the top down: sandstone, shale, limestone, conglomerate. The layers are flat. Which is oldest and which is youngest?
steps: Flat layers have not been overturned, so superposition applies.
The bottom layer, conglomerate, is oldest; the top layer, sandstone, is youngest.
blocks.a: Conglomerate is oldest; sandstone is youngest

blocks.title: Tilted layers
blocks.q: Layers in a cliff tilt at 30°. Were they laid down that way?
steps: Sediment settles in flat layers.
So the layers were tilted after they formed, by Earth movements. The tilting is younger than all of the layers it tilted.

blocks.html: Applying "oldest at the bottom" to layers that were later folded so far that they turned upside down. In an overturned fold, the order is reversed. Geologists check which way was up using clues such as mud cracks or ripple marks, which form on the top surface of a layer.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, Geologic Time: Online Edition (relative time)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS1-4

blocks.html: Layers are not the only things in rock. Magma can squeeze up through cracks and harden into a sheet of igneous rock called a dike, and rock can break and slip along a fault. These features cut across the layers, and that tells their age.
Anything that cuts across rock is younger than the rock it cuts. A dike or fault is younger than every layer it crosses and older than any layer that lies unbroken on top of it.

You can't cut a cake before it is baked. To slice through a layer, the layer must already be there. So a dike that crosses layers A, B and C formed after all three. If layer D lies across the top of the dike, unbroken, then D settled after the dike formed.

blocks.name: es-strata
blocks.cap: Layers, a dike and a fault, lettered. Before you step through the history with Next event, try to put the letters in order: bottom layers first, then whatever cuts them.

blocks.title: Where the dike stops
blocks.q: A dike cuts through layers 1, 2 and 3 but stops at the bottom of layer 4, which lies on top. How old is the dike compared with the layers?
steps: It cuts layers 1, 2 and 3, so it is younger than all three.
Layer 4 lies unbroken on top of it, so layer 4 is younger than the dike.
blocks.a: Younger than layers 1 to 3, older than layer 4

blocks.title: Putting events in order
blocks.q: Flat layers A (bottom) and B (top) are cut by a fault F, and a dike D cuts both layers but is itself broken by the fault. Order the events.
steps: Layers first, bottom up: A, then B.
D cuts both layers: it came next.
F breaks the dike too, so the fault is youngest: A, B, D, F.

blocks.html: Dating a dike by the layer where it ends, as if it were the same age as that layer. A dike must be younger than every layer it cuts across. Check: trace the dike up from the bottom; it is younger than the highest layer it cuts, and older than the layer it stops under.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, Geologic Time: Online Edition (relative time)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS1-4

blocks.html: Superposition and cross-cutting give the order of events. To find ages in years, geologists use radioactive atoms. Some atoms, like uranium-238 and potassium-40, are unstable: one by one they change (decay) into other atoms. Each kind decays at its own steady rate, set by its half-life, the time for half of the atoms to decay.

head: Parent atom
Daughter atom
Half-life
Used to date
rows: Once-living things, up to about 50,000 years old
Crystals in igneous rock, up to the age of Earth
blocks.cap: Some radioactive clocks. (Newer measurements give carbon-14 about 5,700 years; we use 5,730.)

blocks.html: After each half-life, half of the remaining parent atoms are left: $\tfrac{1}{2}$, then $\tfrac{1}{4}$, then $\tfrac{1}{8}$. After $n$ half-lives the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$, and the age is $n$ × the half-life.

Each unstable atom has the same chance of decaying in a given time, no matter how old it is or how many others are around. So in each half-life, half of whatever is left decays. The rate does not change with heat, pressure or chemistry, which makes it a dependable clock. That is multiplying by one half again and again, an exponent: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{2} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}$.

blocks.name: es-halflife
blocks.cap: Each dot is an atom. Step through half-lives and watch the number of parent atoms halve each time, while daughter atoms pile up.

blocks.title: After three half-lives
blocks.q: A sample starts with 800 carbon-14 atoms. How many are left after 3 half-lives, and how many years is that?
steps: Halve three times: $800 \to 400 \to 200 \to 100$.
Or: $800 \times \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 800 \times \tfrac{1}{8} = 100$.

blocks.title: Dating a volcanic rock
blocks.q: A volcanic rock has only $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of its original potassium-40 left. How old is it?
steps: $\tfrac{1}{4} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^2$, so 2 half-lives have passed.
Age: $2 \times 1.25 = 2.5$ billion years.

blocks.html: Thinking all the atoms are gone after two half-lives (half, then the other half). Each half-life halves what is left, not what you started with: after two half-lives, one quarter remains; after three, one eighth. Check: the amount left never reaches exactly zero in a few steps; it keeps halving.
Watch atoms decay one at a time in the Atom Lab.
