Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS1-4

blocks.html: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago (4.54 billion, more exactly). To organize that much time, geologists divide it into eons, eras and periods. The boundaries mostly mark big changes in the life seen in fossils, often mass extinctions, and radioactive dating of volcanic layers gives them ages in years. Relative dating puts the events in order.

head: Time span
Began about
Life
rows: Single cells for most of it; the first simple many-celled life near its end
Animals with shells; fish; the first land plants, insects and four-legged animals
Dinosaurs, the first mammals and birds, flowering plants
Mammals spread and diversify; humans appear about 300,000 years ago
blocks.cap: Rounded ages from the International Chronostratigraphic Chart. The eras of the Phanerozoic eon end with the two largest mass extinctions, about 252 and 66 million years ago.

blocks.html: Earth's 4.6-billion-year history is divided into eons, eras and periods by big changes in life. Most of that time, the Precambrian, came before animals with hard parts; humans arrived only in the last sliver.

Deep time is too long to picture directly, so squeeze it. If all of Earth's history were one calendar year, the Precambrian would last until mid-November, the dinosaurs would vanish on about December 26, and humans would show up around 11:25 p.m. on December 31. The Precambrian is about 88% of the whole story: $(4{,}540 - 539) \div 4{,}540 \approx 0.88$.

blocks.name: es-deep-time
blocks.cap: All of Earth's history squeezed into one year. Switch to one day or a 100-meter field.

blocks.title: Which era?
blocks.q: A fossil of a plant-eating dinosaur is found in rock about 150 million years old. Which era is that?
steps: The Mesozoic runs from 252 to 66 million years ago.
150 million years is between them.

blocks.title: On the calendar
blocks.q: If Earth's 4.6-billion-year history were one year (365 days), how many days before the end of the year did the dinosaurs (other than birds) die out, 66 million years ago?
steps: Fraction of history since then: $66 \div 4{,}600 \approx 0.0143$.
Days: $0.0143 \times 365 \approx 5.2$ days before the end, about December 26.

blocks.html: Thinking people lived alongside dinosaurs. The last dinosaurs other than birds died out about 66 million years ago, and our species appeared about 300,000 years ago, more than 65 million years later. Check the time scale: dinosaurs are Mesozoic; humans are the last moment of the Cenozoic.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, Geologic Time: Online Edition
International Commission on Stratigraphy, International Chronostratigraphic Chart (rounded ages)
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS1-4

blocks.html: Look at a world map and South America's east coast seems to fit into Africa's west coast like puzzle pieces. In 1915 the German scientist Alfred Wegener argued that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, which he named Pangaea, and have slowly drifted apart. He gathered several kinds of evidence.

items: Matching coastlines: the edges of the continental shelves fit even better than the shorelines.

Matching fossils: the small freshwater reptile Mesosaurus is found only in southern Africa and South America; the seed fern Glossopteris in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia. Neither could have crossed an ocean.
Matching rocks and mountains: rock layers and old mountain belts line up across the Atlantic, such as the Appalachians and the mountains of Scotland and Norway.
Ancient glaciers: scratches left by ice sheets about 300 million years ago are found in now-tropical Africa, India and South America, and they point back toward a single ice cap.

blocks.html: Matching coastlines, fossils, rocks and signs of ancient glaciers show the continents were once joined. Today we know whole plates move, ocean floor and all, carrying the continents with them.

Each clue alone could be a coincidence. Together they tell one story: put the continents back together, and the fossil ranges join up, the mountain belts become one belt, and the glacier scratches all point away from one ice cap near the South Pole. Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents, so many scientists doubted him. In the 1960s, maps of the ocean floor showed how the lithosphere moves, and the idea became plate tectonics.

blocks.name: es-plates
blocks.cap: Slide back to 250 million years ago to rebuild Pangaea. The fossil and rock evidence lines up when the continents fit.

blocks.title: A fossil puzzle
blocks.q: Fossils of Mesosaurus, a small reptile that lived in fresh water, are found in Brazil and South Africa, but nowhere else. Why is this evidence for drift?
steps: A small freshwater reptile could not swim across a salty ocean thousands of kilometers wide.
If South America and Africa were joined, its home was one stretch of land and lakes.
blocks.a: The two continents were once joined

blocks.title: Ice in the tropics
blocks.q: Rocks in India, which is now near the equator, show deep scratches from glaciers about 300 million years old. What does this suggest?
steps: Huge ice sheets don't form at the equator.
So India was once much closer to the South Pole, joined to other southern continents, and has since moved.
blocks.a: India has moved far from where it was

blocks.html: Picturing the continents plowing through the ocean floor like ships through water. Whole plates move, and a plate can carry both ocean floor and a continent, like the North American Plate, which reaches from California to the middle of the Atlantic. Check: if continents plowed through the sea floor, it would be crumpled in front of them, and it isn't.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth: Historical Perspective
OpenStax, Astronomy 2e, 8.2 Earth's Crust
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-3

blocks.html: In the 1950s and 1960s, ships mapped the ocean floor and found a mountain range 65,000 km long winding through every ocean: the mid-ocean ridges. Down the middle of each runs a crack where hot rock rises from the mantle, melts a little, and cools into new basalt. This is seafloor spreading, the missing piece of continental drift.
New ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves away on both sides, like two conveyor belts. So the rock gets older the farther it lies from the ridge, in the same pattern on both sides.

Three findings fit together. Rock samples are youngest at the ridge and older farther away. The sediment on the sea floor is thin at the ridge and thicker farther away, because it has had longer to pile up. And stripes of rock magnetized in alternating directions (Earth's magnetic field flips now and then) lie in matching, mirror-image bands on the two sides of the ridge. Each new strip of rock records the field as it cools, then gets carried away.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: New rock forms at the ridge and spreads both ways. Run time forward: the magnetic stripes and ages are mirror images across the ridge.

blocks.title: How old?
blocks.q: A ridge spreads at 2.5 cm a year on each side. How old is ocean floor 100 km from the ridge?
steps: Change 100 km to centimeters: $100 \times 100{,}000 = 10{,}000{,}000$ cm.

blocks.title: Mirror image
blocks.q: Ocean floor 300 km east of a ridge is 12 million years old. How old is the floor 300 km west of it?
steps: Spreading pushes new rock out equally on both sides.
So rock the same distance away on the other side has the same age.

blocks.html: Expecting the ocean floor to hold Earth's oldest rock because the oceans seem so ancient. Almost all ocean floor is younger than about 200 million years, because old ocean floor sinks back into the mantle at trenches. Some continental rock is about 4 billion years old. Check: the oldest sea floor is always far from the ridges, near the edges of the oceans.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth: Developing the Theory
NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Age of the Ocean Floor
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-3

blocks.html: The lithosphere is broken into about a dozen large plates and many small ones. They move a few centimeters a year, and almost all the action happens where they meet: the plate boundaries. There are three kinds.

head: Boundary
Motion
Examples
rows: Plates pull apart; new lithosphere forms
Mid-Atlantic Ridge, Iceland, East African Rift
Plates push together; one sinks under the other (subduction) or they crumple
Plates slide past each other sideways
blocks.cap: The three kinds of plate boundary.

blocks.html: Plates pull apart at divergent boundaries, push together at convergent boundaries and slide past each other at transform boundaries. New lithosphere made at one kind of boundary is balanced by old lithosphere destroyed at another.

Earth is not getting bigger. Every year seafloor spreading makes new lithosphere at divergent boundaries. The same amount must disappear somewhere: at convergent boundaries, dense oceanic lithosphere bends down and sinks back into the mantle. At transform boundaries lithosphere is neither made nor destroyed, only scraped past.

blocks.name: es-plates
blocks.cap: The major plates and their boundaries. Arrows show the direction each plate moves.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: Cross-sections of each kind of boundary. Use the tabs to compare them.

blocks.title: Name the boundary
blocks.q: Along the San Andreas Fault, the Pacific Plate slides northwest past the North American Plate. What kind of boundary is it?
steps: The plates move sideways past each other, neither apart nor together.
That is a transform boundary.

blocks.title: Where does the old floor go?
blocks.q: The Atlantic floor is getting wider. Why isn't Earth getting bigger?
steps: New lithosphere is made at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (divergent).
An equal amount sinks into the mantle at convergent boundaries, such as the trenches around the Pacific.
blocks.a: Lithosphere is destroyed at convergent boundaries

blocks.html: Thinking plates moving apart leave an open gap. Hot rock rises and fills a divergent boundary as fast as the plates separate, so no gap opens. Meanwhile old lithosphere sinks at convergent boundaries, so Earth stays the same size. Check: the ocean floor at a ridge is solid new rock, not a hole.

sources.name: U.S. Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth: Understanding Plate Motions
OpenStax, Astronomy 2e, 8.2 Earth's Crust
Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-3

blocks.html: Each kind of plate boundary builds its own landforms. Knowing the boundary tells you what to expect, and the landforms tell you what kind of boundary lies beneath.

head: Boundary
Landforms
Example
rows: Mid-ocean ridge with a rift down its center
Deep trench and an arc of volcanic islands
Trench offshore and a chain of volcanic mountains
Long faults, offset streams; earthquakes but few volcanoes
blocks.cap: Every kind of boundary has earthquakes; volcanoes come mainly with spreading and with subduction.

blocks.html: Ridges and rift valleys mark divergent boundaries; trenches with volcanic arcs mark subduction; high folded mountains mark continents colliding; long, straight faults mark transform boundaries.

Where an ocean plate meets another plate, the denser ocean plate sinks into a trench. As it goes down, water squeezed out of it lowers the melting point of the mantle above, so magma rises and builds volcanoes in a line parallel to the trench. Continents are too light (buoyant) to sink, so when two collide, neither subducts: the crust crumples and stacks up into the tallest mountains on Earth.

blocks.name: es-boundary
blocks.cap: Compare the cross-sections. Notice where melting happens and where it doesn't.

blocks.title: From landforms to boundary
blocks.q: A deep ocean trench lies just off the coast of a continent, with a chain of volcanoes on land. What kind of boundary is this?
steps: A trench means one plate is sinking: convergent.
Volcanoes on a continent next to it: an ocean plate is sinking under a continental plate.

blocks.title: Why no volcanoes?
blocks.q: The Himalayas have no active volcanoes, even though India is still pushing into Asia. Why?
steps: Both plates carry continents, which are too buoyant to sink.
Without a sinking ocean plate, the mantle doesn't melt, so no magma forms; the crust just crumples and thickens.
blocks.a: No plate is subducting, so no magma forms

blocks.html: Thinking all mountains are volcanoes. The Himalayas and the Alps are crust crumpled and stacked where two continents collide; they have no volcanoes. Check: volcanic mountains are cone-shaped and stand alone or in chains near trenches and rifts, while folded ranges are long belts of bent rock layers.

Next Generation Science Standards, MS-ESS2-3

blocks.html: Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow: a few centimeters a year. That seems like nothing, but plates have been moving for hundreds of millions of years. To see what the motion adds up to, you need careful unit conversions.

head: Unit
Equals
blocks.cap: Conversions you will use.

blocks.html: Distance = rate × time. A handy shortcut: 1 cm per year = 10 km per million years, because 1,000,000 cm = 10 km.

Work in one set of units and the numbers take care of themselves. At 1 cm a year, a million years gives 1,000,000 cm. Divide by 100 to get 10,000 m, then by 1,000 to get 10 km. So 1 cm/yr is the same rate as 10 km per million years. Then 4 cm/yr is 40 km per million years, and in 50 million years that is 2,000 km: enough to open a sea.

blocks.name: es-plates
blocks.cap: GPS stations measure plate motion in millimeters per year. Pick two stations to see how fast they move apart or together.

blocks.title: Two million years
blocks.q: A plate moves 5 cm a year. How far does it move in 2 million years, in kilometers?
steps: Shortcut check: 5 cm/yr = 50 km per million years, × 2 = 100 km.

blocks.title: How long to open an ocean?
blocks.q: Two continents drift apart at 3 cm a year. How long until they are 3,000 km apart?
steps: 3 cm/yr = 30 km per million years.
$3{,}000 \div 30 = 100$ million years.

blocks.html: Losing track of units: 5 cm a year for 2 million years is 10 million centimeters, which is only 100 km, not 10 million km. Check: write the unit next to every number, and convert centimeters to kilometers (divide by 100,000) before you answer.

blocks.html: Along a fault, often near a plate boundary, rocks on the two sides are pushed in different directions but stuck together. They bend slowly, storing energy like a drawn bow, until they snap and slip. The sudden slip sends out vibrations called seismic waves: an earthquake.

items: The focus is the place underground where the rock first breaks. The epicenter is the point on the surface straight above it.
P waves (primary) arrive first. They push and pull the rock in the direction they travel, and they can pass through solids, liquids and gases. In the crust they go about 6 km each second.
S waves (secondary) arrive next. They shake the rock side to side and travel only through solids, at about 3.5 km/s in the crust.
Surface waves arrive last and travel along the ground. They are slowest but often shake hardest and do the most damage.

blocks.html: An earthquake is rock suddenly slipping along a fault. It sends out P waves first, then S waves, then slower surface waves. The break starts at the focus, underground; the epicenter is on the surface above it.

Because P waves outrun S waves, the gap between their arrivals grows the farther you are from the quake, like the gap between two runners at different speeds. Over 84 km, a P wave at 6 km/s takes 14 s and an S wave at 3.5 km/s takes 24 s, a 10 s gap. Measure the gap, and you know the distance. Three stations together pin down the epicenter.

blocks.name: es-seismic
blocks.cap: Watch the waves spread from the focus. The Seismograms tab shows the P–S gap growing at stations farther away.

blocks.title: Which arrives first?
blocks.q: A seismometer 300 km away records an earthquake. Using 6 km/s for P waves and 3 km/s for S waves, when does each arrive?
steps: P wave: $300 \div 6 = 50$ s after the quake.
S wave: $300 \div 3 = 100$ s after the quake.
The S wave arrives 50 s after the P wave.
blocks.a: P after 50 s, S after 100 s

blocks.title: Through the core
blocks.q: Why don't S waves from a large earthquake reach stations on the far side of Earth?
steps: S waves travel only through solids.
The outer core is liquid, so it blocks them, leaving a large "shadow zone" on the far side.
blocks.a: The liquid outer core stops them

blocks.html: Thinking the epicenter is where the rock breaks. The break starts at the focus, which can be a few kilometers or hundreds of kilometers underground. The epicenter is just the point on the map directly above the focus. Check: news reports give an epicenter and a depth; the depth is how far down the focus is.

blocks.html: Earthquakes range from tiny tremors no one feels to giants that shake whole countries. Magnitude measures an earthquake's size with one number. Each step up is a big jump, because the scale uses powers of 10.

Each whole step up in magnitude means seismic waves about 10 times taller on a seismogram and about 32 times more energy released. Two steps means 100 times taller waves and about 1,000 times the energy.

Quake sizes span a huge range, so seismologists use a scale that counts powers of ten, the way an exponent does. Going from magnitude 4 to 6 is two steps: waves $10 \times 10 = 10^2 = 100$ times taller, and energy about $32 \times 32 \approx 1{,}000$ times more. Today the U.S. Geological Survey uses the moment magnitude scale, built from the size of the fault break and how far it slipped, but the steps work the same way.

blocks.name: es-seismic
blocks.cap: Compare two earthquakes. Each block is the energy of the smaller quake; count how many the bigger one needs.

head: Magnitude change
Wave height (amplitude)

blocks.title: How much taller?
blocks.q: A magnitude 6 earthquake and a magnitude 4 earthquake are recorded the same distance away. How many times taller are the bigger one's waves?
steps: The difference is $6 - 4 = 2$ steps.
Each step is × 10: $10^2 = 100$ times taller.

blocks.title: Energy
blocks.q: About how many times more energy does a magnitude 7 release than a magnitude 5?
steps: Two steps up.
About $32 \times 32 \approx 1{,}000$ times the energy.

blocks.html: Reading magnitude like ordinary counting, so a magnitude 6 seems twice a magnitude 3. It is three steps bigger: waves $10^3 = 1{,}000$ times taller and about 32,000 times the energy. Check: subtract the magnitudes first, then multiply by 10 (or by about 32) once for each step.

Magnitude is different from intensity, which describes how strongly the ground shook at one place (the Modified Mercalli scale, I to XII). One earthquake has one magnitude but many intensities: strongest near the epicenter and weaker far away.

blocks.html: A volcano is an opening where magma reaches the surface. How a volcano erupts, and what shape it builds, depends mostly on how runny its magma is and how much gas it holds. Most volcanoes sit along plate boundaries.

head: Type
Magma
Eruptions and shape
Example
rows: Gentle lava flows build a broad, gently sloping mountain
Small, steep cone of loose cinders
Explosive eruptions; tall, steep cone of lava and ash layers
blocks.cap: Main kinds of volcanoes.

blocks.html: Runny, low-silica lava lets gas escape gently and builds broad shield volcanoes. Sticky, high-silica magma traps gas until it bursts out explosively, building steep composite volcanoes.

Silica (SiO₂) makes molecules link into chains, which makes magma thick and sticky, like cold honey. Gas bubbles can't rise easily through sticky magma, so pressure builds until it blasts the magma apart into ash. In runny basalt, bubbles slip out easily, like bubbles in boiling soup, so the lava just pours out. That is why Hawaiian eruptions are mostly gentle while Mount St. Helens exploded in 1980.

blocks.name: es-volcano
blocks.cap: Change the silica and gas and watch the eruption style change. Other tabs show the eruption scale and the hazards.

blocks.title: Predict the eruption
blocks.q: A volcano's magma is high in silica and full of dissolved gas. What kind of eruption should you expect?
steps: High silica: sticky magma.
Gas trapped in sticky magma builds pressure.
Expect explosive eruptions of ash, typical of a composite volcano.

blocks.title: Read the shape
blocks.q: A volcano is about 100 km wide but has slopes of only a few degrees. What kind is it, and what is its lava like?
steps: Broad and gentle means lava flowed far before cooling.
That takes runny, low-silica basalt: a shield volcano.
blocks.a: A shield volcano with runny basalt lava

blocks.html: Thinking lava flows are the main danger. Most lava flows move slowly enough for people to walk away. Fast clouds of hot ash and gas (pyroclastic flows) and volcanic mudflows (lahars) have killed far more people. In 1985 a lahar from Nevado del Ruiz in Colombia killed about 23,000 people.

blocks.html: Most volcanoes sit at plate boundaries, but Hawaii is in the middle of the Pacific Plate, thousands of kilometers from any boundary. It sits over a hot spot: a place where unusually hot mantle rock rises and melts, staying put while the plate slides over it.

A plate moving over a fixed hot spot carries each volcano away from the heat and builds a new one, leaving a line of volcanoes that get older with distance. The ages and distances give the plate's speed and direction.

Think of a sheet of paper slid slowly over a candle: it gets a line of scorch marks, and the oldest mark is farthest from the flame. In Hawaii the Big Island, over the hot spot, has active volcanoes. Toward the northwest, Maui, Oahu and Kauai are older and more worn down. Kauai's oldest lavas are about 5 million years old, about 500 km from the hot spot, so the Pacific Plate has moved about 500 km in 5 million years: about 10 cm a year (using plate rates).

blocks.name: es-plates
blocks.cap: The Hawaiian–Emperor chain. Move the plate over the hot spot and watch new islands form while old ones drift away and sink.

blocks.title: Plate speed
blocks.q: An island 300 km from a hot spot is 3 million years old. How fast has the plate moved, in cm per year?
steps: Speed = distance ÷ time = $300 \div 3 = 100$ km per million years.
1 cm/yr = 10 km per million years, so 100 km per million years = 10 cm/yr.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: In a chain of hot-spot islands, the active volcano is at the southeast end and the islands get older toward the northwest. Which way is the plate moving?
steps: The oldest islands have been carried farthest from the hot spot.
They lie to the northwest, so the plate is moving northwest.

blocks.html: Assuming every volcano sits on a plate boundary. Hot-spot volcanoes like Hawaii and Yellowstone are in the middle of plates. Check: a hot-spot chain gets older in a steady line away from the active end, which boundary volcanoes don't do.

blocks.html: No one can say the exact day an earthquake will strike. But scientists can say where hazards happen and how often, and for volcanoes they can often spot warning signs weeks or months ahead. That is the difference between a prediction (a specific time and place) and a forecast (a chance over a span of time).

items: Earthquakes: records of past quakes and fault slip give the chance of a large quake in a region over decades. The U.S. Geological Survey estimated a 72% chance of at least one magnitude 6.7 or larger quake in the San Francisco Bay Area between 2014 and 2043.
Volcanoes: rising magma causes swarms of small earthquakes, swelling of the ground (measured with tilt meters and GPS) and more volcanic gas. These signs often come before eruptions.
Early warning: systems such as ShakeAlert detect the fast P waves of a quake that has already started and send alerts seconds before the stronger shaking arrives.

blocks.html: Forecasts give the chance of a hazard over a time span, based on records and warning signs. If an event happens on average once every $T$ years, the chance in any one year is about $\tfrac{1}{T}$.

Faults load up with stress over decades to centuries and release it at irregular times, so the exact date can't be known. But the long-term average can. If a fault has had 5 large quakes in 1,000 years, the average gap (recurrence interval) is $1{,}000 \div 5 = 200$ years, and the chance in any one year is about $\tfrac{1}{200}$, or 0.5%. That chance helps communities decide how strongly to build.

blocks.name: es-chance
blocks.cap: Simulate many 30-year stretches with a 1-in-100 yearly chance. Some stretches have no event, some have two: chance, not a schedule.

blocks.title: Recurrence
blocks.q: A town's records show 4 big floods in 120 years. What is the average time between floods, and the chance of one in any year?
steps: Average interval: $120 \div 4 = 30$ years.
Yearly chance: $\tfrac{1}{30}$, about 3.3%.
blocks.a: About 30 years; about a 1 in 30 chance each year

blocks.title: Volcano signs
blocks.q: Around a quiet volcano, small earthquakes become frequent, the ground starts to bulge and gas output rises. What do these signs suggest?
steps: All three signs come from magma moving up into the volcano.
An eruption may be coming; scientists raise the alert level, though it may still be weeks away or may not happen.
blocks.a: Magma is rising; an eruption may be coming

blocks.html: Believing scientists can predict the exact day of an earthquake. No one can yet; forecasts give the chance of a quake over years or decades. A related trap: a "100-year flood" is not one that comes exactly every 100 years. It has a 1% chance every year, so two can happen in back-to-back years.

blocks.html: Earth is called the blue planet: oceans cover about 71% of its surface. Water is part of the hydrosphere, and almost all of it is salty. The fresh water that people, plants and land animals use is a small slice, and most of that slice is locked away.

head: Where the water is
Share of all water
Share of fresh water
rows: Lakes, rivers, swamps, soil, air and living things
blocks.cap: Rounded from the U.S. Geological Survey (after Gleick, 1996). About 97% of all water is salty and about 2.5% is fresh.

blocks.html: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water, nearly all in the oceans. Of the small share that is fresh, about two-thirds is frozen in ice and nearly one-third is underground; lakes and rivers hold only a tiny part.

Imagine all of Earth's water as 1,000 liters. Using percents, the fresh water is 2.5% of it: 25 L. Of that, 69% is ice ($25 \times 0.69 \approx 17$ L) and 30% is groundwater (about 7.5 L). All the lakes and rivers together are only about 0.27% of the fresh water: about 70 mL, less than half a cup.

blocks.name: es-water
blocks.cap: The bars show where Earth's water is. Check "Fresh water only" to see how small the lakes and rivers are, even among fresh water.

blocks.title: A model of the water
blocks.q: In a model where all of Earth's water is 2,000 L, about 2.5% is fresh. How many liters is that, and about how much of it is ice (69%)?
steps: Fresh water: $2{,}000 \times 0.025 = 50$ L.
blocks.a: 50 L fresh, about 34.5 L of it ice

blocks.title: Where is most fresh water?
blocks.q: Is most of Earth's fresh water in lakes and rivers?
steps: Ice holds about 69% and groundwater about 30%: together about 99%.
Lakes and rivers hold well under 1% of the fresh water.
blocks.a: No: it is mostly ice and groundwater

blocks.html: Thinking most fresh water is in lakes and rivers, because that is the water we see. They hold well under 1% of it. Most fresh water is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers or hidden underground. Check: add the ice (69%) and groundwater (30%) shares, and almost nothing is left over.

blocks.html: Earth's water is always on the move, between the oceans, the air, the land and living things. This endless loop is the water cycle, and two things power it: energy from the Sun and the pull of gravity.

items: Evaporation: sunlight warms water, which turns into invisible water vapor. Plants also give off vapor through their leaves (transpiration).
Condensation: rising air cools, and vapor condenses into tiny droplets or ice crystals: clouds.
Precipitation: droplets grow and fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail.
Runoff flows downhill into streams, lakes and the sea; infiltration soaks into the ground to become groundwater.

blocks.html: The Sun's energy lifts water into the air by evaporation; cooling turns the vapor into clouds; gravity brings it back down as precipitation and pulls it downhill as runoff and groundwater.

Turning liquid water into vapor takes a lot of energy, and sunlight supplies it, mostly over the oceans. Vapor rides up with rising, convecting air and cools, so it condenses into droplets. Gravity does the rest: it pulls drops out of clouds and pulls water downhill over and under the land. A water molecule spends on average about 9 days in the air, but about 3,000 years in the ocean.

blocks.name: es-water
blocks.cap: Turn on "Sun or gravity?" to color each step by what powers it. Press play to watch water move.

blocks.title: A puddle disappears
blocks.q: A puddle dries up on a sunny afternoon. Where did the water go, and what powered it?
steps: The water evaporated into the air as invisible water vapor.
The energy came from sunlight warming the puddle.
blocks.a: Into the air as vapor, powered by the Sun

blocks.title: Sun or gravity?
blocks.q: Which steps are driven by gravity: evaporation, precipitation, runoff, transpiration?
steps: Evaporation and transpiration lift water up as vapor: powered by the Sun.
Precipitation falls and runoff flows downhill: pulled by gravity.

blocks.html: Thinking clouds are made of water vapor. Water vapor is an invisible gas, part of the air. Clouds are tiny drops of liquid water or ice crystals, which is why you can see them. Check: the "steam" above a kettle is visible because the vapor has already condensed into droplets; right at the spout, where it is still vapor, the air looks clear.

blocks.html: When rain soaks into the ground, it trickles down through tiny spaces between grains of soil and rock. Deep enough, every space is full of water. That water is groundwater, about 30% of Earth's fresh water, fed by the infiltration step of the water cycle.

items: The unsaturated zone: near the surface, the spaces hold both air and water.
The water table: the top of the zone where every space is filled with water.
The saturated zone: below the water table, all the spaces are full.
An aquifer: a layer of rock or sediment that holds water and lets it flow, such as sand, gravel or sandstone. Wells are drilled into aquifers, below the water table.

blocks.html: Groundwater fills the tiny spaces in soil and rock. Porosity is how much open space a material has; permeability is how easily water flows through it. A good aquifer needs both.

Porosity is a percent: pore volume ÷ total volume. Clay has high porosity, often around 50%, but its pores are so tiny that water barely moves through them: low permeability. Sand and gravel have less pore space, 25 to 40%, but the pores are large and connected, so water flows easily. That makes sand and gravel good aquifers and clay a barrier.

blocks.name: es-water
blocks.cap: Pump well A and watch the water table sag into a cone around it. If the cone drops below a nearby well, that well can go dry.

blocks.title: Measuring porosity
blocks.q: A 500 cm³ jar of dry gravel can hold 150 cm³ of water poured into its spaces. What is its porosity?
steps: Porosity = pore volume ÷ total volume.

blocks.title: Where to drill
blocks.q: Layer 1 is clay; layer 2 below it is sand; the water table is 20 m down, in the sand. Where should a well end?
steps: The well must reach below the water table, where the spaces are full of water.
It should end in the sand, which lets water flow in; clay would give very little.

blocks.html: Picturing groundwater as underground lakes and rivers. Except in caves, groundwater mostly fills tiny spaces between grains. Also, porosity (how much space) is not permeability (how easily water flows): clay is very porous but holds its water tightly. Check: a good aquifer is both porous and permeable.

blocks.html: The atmosphere is a thin layer of gases held to Earth by gravity. Dry air (with the water vapor left out) has almost the same recipe everywhere near the ground.

head: Gas
Share of dry air
blocks.cap: Dry air, rounded (NOAA; carbon dioxide from the Mauna Loa record, 2024). Real air also holds water vapor, from almost 0% to about 4%, which changes with place and weather.

blocks.html: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% argon. Carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%, yet it matters a lot for climate and for plants.

"Parts per million" (ppm) is a percent with a bigger denominator. 420 ppm means 420 out of every 1,000,000 molecules, which is $420 \div 1{,}000{,}000 = 0.00042$, or 0.042%. Out of every 10,000 molecules of air, only about 4 are carbon dioxide, but those few absorb heat (the greenhouse effect) and feed every plant on Earth.

blocks.name: es-atmosphere
blocks.cap: The pie shows the gases in dry air. Nitrogen and oxygen make up 99%.

blocks.title: Oxygen in a room
blocks.q: A classroom holds 200,000 liters of air. About how many liters are oxygen?
steps: Oxygen is about 21% of air: a percent of a number.

blocks.title: From ppm to percent
blocks.q: Before the 1800s, air held about 280 ppm of carbon dioxide. What percent is that?

blocks.html: Thinking air is mostly oxygen, or that carbon dioxide is a big part of it. Air is mostly nitrogen (78%); oxygen is about a fifth, and carbon dioxide only about 0.04%. Check: the shares must add up to about 100%, and 78 + 21 + 1 already does, leaving very little room for anything else.

blocks.html: Go up through the atmosphere and the air thins out. The temperature does something stranger: it falls, rises, falls and rises again. Those turns mark four layers.

Height (about)
Temperature going up
What happens there

Auroras; the International Space Station orbits here
blocks.cap: The layers of the atmosphere (heights vary with latitude and season: the troposphere is about 8 km deep near the poles and 16 to 18 km near the equator).

blocks.html: Temperature changes direction with height, marking four layers: troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone), mesosphere (coldest) and thermosphere (very thin and hot).

The troposphere is warmed from below by the sunlit ground, so it gets colder as you go up. In the stratosphere, ozone absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet light, which heats that layer from within, so it gets warmer with height. Above the ozone the heating stops and the air cools again. At the top, the few molecules of the thermosphere absorb the most energetic sunlight and move very fast, which is what a high temperature means.

blocks.name: es-atmosphere
blocks.cap: Drag the probe up through the atmosphere and watch the temperature turn, layer by layer.

blocks.title: A mountain hike
blocks.q: At the base of a mountain it is 20 °C. In the troposphere, air cools about 6.5 °C for each kilometer up. About how warm is it at the top, 2 km higher?
steps: Cooling: $2 \times 6.5 = 13$ °C.

blocks.title: Which layer?
blocks.q: A meteor glows and burns up about 70 km above the ground. Which layer is it in?
steps: The mesosphere runs from about 50 to 85 km.
70 km is inside it.

blocks.html: Expecting the air to get colder all the way up. It does in the troposphere, but ozone warms the stratosphere, and the thin thermosphere is very hot. Check: a temperature graph of the atmosphere zigzags; it is not a straight line.
"Hot" in the thermosphere does not mean you would feel warm there: the air is so thin that very few fast molecules would hit you, so you would lose heat and feel cold.

blocks.html: Air has mass and weight. The whole column of air above you, all the way up through the atmosphere, presses down on everything below it. That push spread over an area is air pressure. At sea level it is about 1,013 hectopascals (hPa), or about 10 newtons on every square centimeter: like the weight of a 1 kg bag on each fingernail-sized patch.
Air pressure is the weight of the air above, spread over an area. It is highest at sea level and drops with height, falling to about half for every 5.5 km you go up. It pushes in every direction.

Air is a gas, and gases can be squeezed. The air near the ground holds up all the air above it, so it is packed tightest, and its density is highest there. Climb higher and there is less air above you pushing down, so the pressure and density both drop. Because air molecules zoom around in all directions, they push on surfaces sideways and upward too, not only down.

blocks.name: es-atmosphere
blocks.cap: Move the probe up and read the pressure: about half of sea-level pressure at 5.5 km, and a quarter at 11 km.

blocks.title: Halving with height
blocks.q: Sea-level pressure is about 1,000 hPa. About what is the pressure 11 km up?
steps: 11 km is two steps of 5.5 km.
Halve twice: $1{,}000 \to 500 \to 250$ hPa.

blocks.title: The push on a book
blocks.q: Air pushes about 10 N on each square centimeter. A book cover is 20 cm by 25 cm. How hard does the air push on it?
steps: Area: $20 \times 25 = 500$ cm².
Force: $500 \times 10 = 5{,}000$ N, as much as the weight of about 500 kg. The air under the book pushes up just as hard, so it doesn't move.

blocks.html: Thinking air weighs nothing, or that air pressure only pushes down. Air pushes in every direction, and the air and fluids inside our bodies push back out just as hard, which is why we don't feel crushed. Check: a sealed bag of chips puffs up on a mountain, because the air pressure outside it is lower there.
See pressure come from molecules hitting the walls in the Gas Lab.

blocks.html: Wind is air moving from where the pressure is higher to where it is lower. Those pressure differences come from uneven heating: warm air expands and rises, making lower pressure near the ground, while cool, dense air sinks, making higher pressure. It is convection in the air.

Uneven heating makes pressure differences, and air flows from high pressure toward low pressure. The bigger the difference over a distance, the stronger the wind. A wind is named for the direction it comes from.

At the coast on a sunny day, land heats up faster than water. Air over the land warms, expands and rises, leaving lower pressure near the ground. Cooler, denser air over the sea flows in to replace it: a sea breeze, blowing from sea to land. At night the land cools faster than the water, the pattern flips, and a land breeze blows from land to sea.

blocks.name: es-wind
blocks.cap: Lines of equal pressure (isobars). Where they are close together, the pressure changes fast and the wind is strong.

blocks.title: Naming a wind
blocks.q: A wind blows from the north toward the south. What is it called, and what is its direction in degrees?
steps: Winds are named for where they come from: a north wind.
Wind direction is the compass bearing it comes from: north is 0° (or 360°).

blocks.title: Day or night?
blocks.q: At a beach, a breeze blows from the land out to sea. Is it more likely day or night?
steps: Air flows from high to low pressure.
Flow from land to sea means lower pressure over the sea: the sea is warmer than the land, which happens at night.

blocks.html: Naming a wind by where it is going. A north wind blows from the north, toward the south. Check: weather reports give the direction the wind comes from, and wind vanes point into the wind, toward its source.

blocks.html: The Sun heats Earth unevenly: most strongly near the equator, where it is high in the sky, and least near the poles (as with the seasons). This uneven heating drives winds on a planet-wide scale, and Earth's spin bends them into steady belts.

items: Near the equator, warm, moist air rises: a belt of low pressure, clouds and heavy rain.
The air spreads toward the poles high up, cools, and sinks near 30° N and 30° S: high pressure and dry air, which is why many great deserts lie near 30°.
At the surface, air flows back toward the equator as the trade winds. Between 30° and 60° the westerlies blow; near the poles, the polar easterlies.

blocks.html: Uneven heating makes air rise at the equator and sink near 30°. Earth's spin bends moving air (the Coriolis effect): to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, turning the flow into the trade winds, westerlies and polar easterlies.

Earth spins toward the east, and the ground at the equator moves faster (about 1,670 km/h) than the ground nearer the poles. Air moving toward the equator from 30° N can't keep up with the faster ground beneath it, so it lags behind toward the west: seen from the ground, it curves to the right and arrives as a wind from the northeast. That is the northeast trade wind. In the Southern Hemisphere the curve goes the other way, making southeast trades.

blocks.name: es-wind
blocks.cap: The global wind belts. The Turntable tab shows why a straight path looks curved on a spinning Earth.

blocks.title: Trade winds
blocks.q: Which way do the trade winds blow just north of the equator?
steps: Surface air flows from about 30° N toward the equator, so it starts out moving south.
In the Northern Hemisphere it is bent to the right, toward the west.
So it comes from the northeast: the northeast trades.

blocks.title: Deserts
blocks.q: Why are the Sahara and the Australian deserts near 30° latitude?
steps: Air that rose at the equator sinks near 30°.
Sinking air warms and dries out, so clouds rarely form there.

blocks.html: Thinking the Coriolis effect makes sinks drain in opposite directions in the two hemispheres. It is far too weak at the size of a sink, which drains whichever way the water was already swirling. It matters only for large, long-lasting motions such as winds, ocean currents and hurricanes.

blocks.html: An air mass is a huge body of air, often over a thousand kilometers across, that has taken on the temperature and moisture of the region where it sat. Winds carry air masses away from home, and where two different ones meet, the boundary is a front.

head: Air mass
Formed over
Character
Example for North America
rows: Deserts of Mexico and the Southwest
blocks.cap: Continental means dry; maritime means moist; polar means cold; tropical means warm.

blocks.html: Where two air masses meet, the denser, colder air stays low and the warmer air is lifted over it. Rising air cools, its water vapor condenses, and clouds and precipitation form along the front.

Cold air is denser, so it hugs the ground like a wedge. At a cold front, cold air plows under warm air and shoves it up steeply: tall clouds, short heavy showers or thunderstorms, then cooler, drier air. At a warm front, warm air slides gently up over the retreating cold air: wide sheets of layered clouds and long, steady rain, then warmer, more humid air. The lifting is the same condensation step of the water cycle.

blocks.name: es-weather-map
blocks.cap: A cross-section through a front. Switch between cold and warm fronts and compare the slope and the clouds. The Map tab shows fronts moving across a weather map.

blocks.title: Name the air mass
blocks.q: An air mass forms over the Gulf of Mexico. What is it like?
steps: Over an ocean: maritime, so moist.
In the warm south: tropical, so warm.
Maritime tropical (mT): warm and humid.

blocks.title: After the front
blocks.q: A line of thunderstorms passes, the wind shifts, and the next day is cooler and drier. What kind of front passed?
steps: Short, heavy storms point to steep lifting.
Cooler, drier air behind it means cold air moved in.
A cold front.

blocks.html: Thinking warm and cold air mix right away at a front. The denser cold air stays low and wedges under the warm air, lifting it. That lifting, not mixing, is what makes the clouds. Check: fronts are drawn as sharp lines on weather maps because the two air masses stay separate for days.

blocks.html: The ocean's surface is always moving. Steady global winds drag the top hundred meters or so of water along, and Earth's spin and the shapes of the continents turn these flows into huge loops called gyres.

items: Gyres turn clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
On the western side of each ocean, currents carry warm water from the tropics toward the poles, like the Gulf Stream along the U.S. East Coast.
On the eastern side, currents carry cool water toward the equator, like the California Current along the U.S. West Coast.

blocks.html: Surface currents are driven mainly by steady winds and turned by Earth's spin into gyres. They move heat: warm currents carry it toward the poles, and cool currents bring cold water toward the equator.

In the North Atlantic, the trade winds push water west near the equator and the westerlies push it east farther north. Between them the water circles around, and the Coriolis effect bends it to the right, giving a clockwise loop. Water flowing north from the tropics along the western side brings tropical warmth with it; water flowing south along the eastern side has been cooled at high latitudes.

blocks.title: Warm or cool?
blocks.q: The Gulf Stream flows north along the east coast of the United States. Is it warm or cool, and why?
steps: It flows from the tropics toward the pole.
So it carries warm tropical water: a warm current.

blocks.title: A coastal climate
blocks.q: San Francisco, next to the cool California Current, often has foggy, cool summers. Why?
steps: The current brings cool water from the north.
Air over the cool water is chilled, and its water vapor condenses into fog that drifts ashore.
blocks.a: The cool current chills the air above it

blocks.html: Thinking tides or the Moon drive ocean currents. Tides only move water back and forth twice a day. Surface currents are pushed mainly by steady winds and turned by Earth's spin. Check: the gyres line up with the global wind belts, not with the Moon.

blocks.html: Below the wind-driven surface currents, the deep ocean also moves, slowly. These deep currents are driven by density differences, like convection: cold, salty water is dense, so it sinks.

Cold water and salty water are denser. Near the poles, surface water becomes cold and salty enough to sink, then creeps along the ocean floor. This drives a slow loop through every ocean, often called the global conveyor belt.

Cooling packs water molecules closer together, raising density. Salt adds mass to the same volume, raising it too. Near Greenland and Antarctica, winter air chills the surface water, and when sea ice forms it leaves most of its salt behind in the water below. That water becomes the densest in the ocean and sinks to the bottom. It flows toward the equator along the sea floor and slowly rises in other oceans. One trip around the loop takes about 1,000 years.

blocks.cap: Convection in the ocean: water chilled near a pole sinks and creeps along the bottom toward the equator.

blocks.title: Which sinks?
blocks.q: Sample A is 2 °C and very salty. Sample B is 20 °C and less salty. Which sinks below the other?
steps: Colder water is denser, and saltier water is denser.
Sample A is both colder and saltier, so it is denser and sinks.

blocks.title: Sea ice and salt
blocks.q: When seawater freezes into sea ice, most of the salt stays in the water. What happens to the water just under the ice?
steps: It gets saltier, and it is already near freezing.
Cold and salty means very dense, so it sinks, feeding the deep current.

blocks.html: Thinking salt makes water lighter, or that the deep ocean sits still. Dissolved salt adds mass, so salty water is denser than fresh water at the same temperature (an egg can float in very salty water). And the deep water moves, slowly, all around the globe. Check: deep water forms only where surface water is both cold and salty.

blocks.html: Weather is what the air is doing at one place and time: today's temperature, wind, clouds and rain, shaped by the air masses and fronts passing by. Climate is the pattern of weather over a long time, usually 30 years or more. Weather is your mood today; climate is your personality.
Weather changes from hour to hour and day to day. Climate is the long-term average and range of weather, usually figured over 30 years. One hot or cold day, week or even year is weather, not climate.

Any single day is a mix of a long-term pattern and a lot of short-term ups and downs. Taking the mean over many years makes the ups and downs cancel out, leaving the pattern. That is why NOAA describes each place's climate with 30-year averages, called climate normals (the current ones cover 1991 to 2020).

blocks.cap: A climograph: average monthly temperature (line) and precipitation (bars), from 30 years of records. Try other cities.

blocks.title: Weather or climate?
blocks.q: Sort these: (1) "It's snowing in Denver right now." (2) "Phoenix gets about 20 cm of rain a year."
steps: (1) describes one moment in one place: weather.
(2) describes a long-term average: climate.

blocks.title: Finding a mean
blocks.q: A town's July average temperatures for five years were 24, 26, 23, 25 and 27 °C. What is the mean?
steps: Divide by 5: $125 \div 5 = 25$ °C.
A real climate normal would use 30 years, not 5.

blocks.html: Treating one cold week as evidence against a warming climate. A cold week is weather. Climate change shows up in long-term averages over decades. Check: ask what time span the evidence covers; if it is days or weeks, it is weather.

blocks.html: Why is Seattle mild and rainy while Chicago, a bit farther south, has bitter winters and hot summers? A place's climate depends on several factors working together.

items: Latitude: closer to the equator, the Sun is higher and it is warmer.
Elevation: higher places are cooler, about 6.5 °C for each kilometer up.
Distance from the ocean: water warms and cools slowly, so coasts have milder winters and cooler summers; inland places have bigger swings.
Ocean currents: a warm current warms nearby land; a cool current cools it.
Mountains: air rising over a range drops its rain on the windward side; the far side lies in a dry "rain shadow."
Prevailing winds: winds blowing off the ocean bring the ocean's mildness and moisture inland.

blocks.html: Latitude sets the starting point, but elevation, distance from the sea, ocean currents, mountains and winds can change a climate a lot. Places at the same latitude can have very different climates.

Water has a high specific heat: it takes a lot of energy to change its temperature. So the ocean warms slowly in summer and cools slowly in winter, and winds off the ocean carry that steadiness to the coast. Far inland, the ground heats and cools quickly, so summers are hotter and winters colder. Mountains add another twist: air forced up their slopes cools, and its vapor condenses into rain, so the air that crosses to the other side is dry.

blocks.title: Up the mountain
blocks.q: A town at sea level averages 24 °C in July. About what is the July average in a mountain town at 2,000 m, nearby?
steps: 2,000 m is 2 km.
Cooling: $2 \times 6.5 = 13$ °C.

blocks.title: Coast or inland?
blocks.q: Two towns at the same latitude: town A has a 10 °C difference between its warmest and coldest months; town B has 35 °C. Which is on the coast?
steps: The ocean evens out temperatures.
The smaller swing, 10 °C, belongs to the coastal town.

blocks.html: Expecting places at the same latitude to share a climate. London and Calgary are at nearly the same latitude, but London's January average is around 5 °C while Calgary's is below −5 °C. London sits near the ocean, warmed by the North Atlantic Current and by winds off the sea; Calgary is far inland at about 1,000 m. Check every factor, not only latitude.

blocks.html: Earth's average surface temperature, a basic fact of its climate, is about 15 °C. If Earth had no greenhouse gases, it would be about −18 °C, frozen over (NASA). The difference comes from the greenhouse effect, and it starts with two kinds of light.

items: Sunlight, mostly visible light, passes through the air and warms the ground and ocean.
The warmed surface gives off energy as infrared light, which we can't see.
Greenhouse gases, such as water vapor, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, absorb much of that infrared and give it off again in all directions, including back down.
So the surface receives energy from both the Sun and the warm air above it, and it warms until it gives off as much energy as it gets.

blocks.html: The greenhouse effect: sunlight warms the surface, the surface gives off infrared, and greenhouse gases absorb some of that infrared and send part of it back down, keeping the surface warmer. More greenhouse gas means a warmer surface.

Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of the air, let infrared pass right through. Molecules with three or more atoms, like CO₂ and H₂O, can bend and stretch in ways that absorb infrared. That is why a gas that is only 0.04% of the air matters so much. Adding more CO₂ makes the air absorb more of the outgoing infrared, so Earth has to warm up to send the same amount of energy back to space. How much warmer Earth gets this century depends on how much more is added.

blocks.cap: A model with one layer of greenhouse gas. Raise how much infrared it absorbs and watch the surface warm. The Spectrum tab shows sunlight and Earth's infrared side by side.

blocks.title: How much warmer?
blocks.q: With greenhouse gases, Earth's average surface temperature is about 15 °C; without them it would be about −18 °C. How much warming do they provide?
steps: About 33 °C of warming.

blocks.title: Which light?
blocks.q: Do greenhouse gases mainly block incoming sunlight or outgoing infrared?
steps: Sunlight (mostly visible) passes through the air almost freely.
Greenhouse gases absorb the infrared that the warmed surface gives off.

blocks.html: Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole, or thinking greenhouse gases trap incoming sunlight. The ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet light high in the stratosphere; the ozone hole is a separate problem. Greenhouse gases absorb the infrared that the warmed Earth gives off. Check: the greenhouse effect works even at night, when no sunlight is coming in at all.

blocks.html: The greenhouse effect predicts that adding carbon dioxide should warm Earth. Many independent measurements show that it has. Scientists trust the conclusion because so many different records point the same way.

items: Air temperature: averaged over the globe, the decade 2011 to 2020 was about 1.1 °C warmer than 1850 to 1900. Each of the last four decades was warmer than any decade before it since 1850 (IPCC).
Carbon dioxide: about 280 parts per million before the 1800s; above 420 ppm in recent years, measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii (NOAA).
Sea level: rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018, as ocean water warmed and expanded and land ice melted (IPCC).
Ice: glaciers are shrinking around the world, and Arctic sea ice in late summer covers far less area than when satellite records began in 1979.

blocks.html: Thermometer records, rising seas, shrinking ice and the rising carbon dioxide record all show that Earth has warmed over the last century, by about 1.1 °C. The warming shows in averages over decades, not in any single year.

Single years bounce up and down with weather patterns such as El Niño, so one year can be cooler than the year before. Averages over 10 or 30 years smooth out the bounces and reveal the trend. The scientific assessment (IPCC, 2021) concludes it is unequivocal that human activities, mainly burning fossil fuels, have warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.

blocks.title: Rate of rise
blocks.q: Carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa was about 340 ppm in 1980 and about 420 ppm in 2023. What was the average rise per year?
steps: $80 \div 43 \approx 1.9$ ppm per year.

blocks.title: How much more?
blocks.q: By what percent has carbon dioxide risen from 280 ppm to 420 ppm?
steps: Increase: $420 - 280 = 140$ ppm.

blocks.html: Judging the trend from one hot or cold year. Years bounce up and down; the warming shows in averages over decades. Check: compare the average of one decade with the average of another, not one year with the next.

blocks.html: Everything we use comes from Earth: water from rivers and aquifers, metals from ores, energy from sunlight, wind and fuels, and stone and sand from the rock cycle. Resources fall into two groups by how fast nature replaces them.

head: Renewable: replaced within a human lifetime
Nonrenewable: took millions of years to form
rows: Coal, oil and natural gas (fossil fuels)
Metal ores, such as copper and iron
Water in rivers and shallow aquifers (if not overused)
Water in some deep aquifers that refill only over thousands of years
blocks.cap: Some resources can be either, depending on how fast we use them.

blocks.html: Renewable resources are replaced by nature within a human lifetime; nonrenewable ones took millions of years to form. Both are spread unevenly, because they are found only where past geologic processes put them.

Geology decides where resources are. Oil and natural gas formed from tiny sea creatures buried in sediment and slowly cooked by Earth's heat over millions of years, so they lie in thick piles of sedimentary rock. Much coal comes from swamp plants buried about 300 million years ago. Many metal ores were left by hot water flowing through cracks near cooling magma. These processes are far too slow to refill what we use in a lifetime.

blocks.name: es-water
blocks.cap: Pumping a well faster than rain refills the aquifer lowers the water table. Some aquifers take thousands of years to refill.

blocks.title: How long will it last?
blocks.q: A region has an estimated 600 million tonnes of a mineral it can mine, and it mines 20 million tonnes a year. At that rate, how many years will it last?
steps: Years = amount available ÷ amount used each year.
$600 \div 20 = 30$ years.

blocks.title: An aquifer's budget
blocks.q: An aquifer gains about 2 million m³ of water a year from rain soaking in, and wells pump out 5 million m³ a year. What happens to the water stored in it each year?
steps: Change = water in − water out = $2 - 5 = -3$ million m³.
It loses about 3 million m³ a year, and the water table drops.
blocks.a: It shrinks by about 3 million m³ a year

blocks.html: Thinking resources are spread evenly, or that groundwater always refills quickly. Ores, oil and good aquifers lie only where past geologic processes put them, and some aquifers, like parts of the High Plains aquifer under the Great Plains, are being pumped much faster than they refill. Check: ask how long nature takes to replace a resource, and compare it with how fast we use it.

blocks.html: About 8 billion people now live on Earth. Each person uses water, energy, food and resources, and produces waste. How much people change Earth's systems depends on two things: how many people there are, and how much each person uses on average.
Total use = number of people × use per person. A change in either one changes the total, and changes in both multiply together.

Picture the total as the area of a rectangle: its width is the number of people and its height is the use per person. Double the width and the area doubles; double the height and it doubles too; do both and it is four times as big. Shrink one while the other grows and the area can stay the same. That is why scientists look at both how many people there are and how resources are used.

blocks.name: earthsci-impact
blocks.cap: Total use is the area of the rectangle. Change the number of people or the use per person and compare with the dashed starting rectangle.

blocks.title: Total water use
blocks.q: A town of 20,000 people uses about 300 liters of water per person each day. How much does the town use in a day?
steps: Total = people × use per person.

blocks.title: Two changes at once
blocks.q: A city's population grows by 20% while each person's energy use falls by 25%. Does the total go up or down, and by how much?
steps: People are multiplied by 1.20; use per person by 0.75.
Total is multiplied by $1.20 \times 0.75 = 0.90$.
So the total falls by 10%.

blocks.html: Blaming impact on the number of people alone, or on how much each person uses alone. The total depends on both, multiplied together. Check with numbers: if the population doubles while use per person halves, the total stays the same.
Engineers and scientists also work on how impacts happen: using water more efficiently, cleaner energy, recycling metals. Those change the use per person, the second factor.
